--- description: >- Harvest builds the apex of the robot data pyramid — embodiment-matched teleoperation data, collected in the US, delivered in GR00T LeRobot. --- # Harvest ## What this company is Robot foundation models are bottlenecked on a kind of data that does not exist yet. Language models inherited the internet. Robots inherited nothing — the synchronized record of vision, proprioception, force and action that a policy needs to learn manipulation was never written down anywhere, because until recently there was no reason to write it down. Harvest manufactures that record. We run human operators teleoperating Unitree G1 humanoids through structured task programs, and we deliver the result as clean, annotated, licensed training corpora in the format buyers' training stacks already ingest. One sentence version: > **We turn operator hours into embodiment-matched demonstration episodes, and we sell them under a buyer-owned commercial license.** ## Why this is a real business right now Three things are simultaneously true in 2026, and the intersection is the opportunity. **The scarcity is documented and quantified.** Scale AI's September 2025 framing — that all open-source robotics datasets combined offered only about 5,000 hours of interaction data — remains the most-cited number in the field. Ken Goldberg's Science Robotics calculation puts it starker: vision-language models already trained on roughly 100,000 years of human-equivalent experience, while the largest reported robot teleoperation dataset amounts to about one year. **The buyers are funded and buying.** Scale AI reported delivering over 150,000 hours of physical-AI data in 2025. XDOF launched in June 2026 with $70M and roughly 20 customers including unnamed frontier labs. Mecka reports a \~$100M run rate. Lightwheel reported RMB 550M of new orders in Q1 2026 alone. This is a market with revenue in it today, not a market waiting on a thesis. **The hardware crossed the affordability line.** The G1 is the first genuinely capable bipedal humanoid you can order on a credit card. Sergey Levine's own cost curve tells the story: the research arm he used in 2014 cost $400,000; Physical Intelligence's current arms cost about $3,000 each. Cheap bodies mean fleets. Fleets mean data. ## The four workstreams
WorkstreamWhat it answers
The Data BusinessHow an episode goes from a G1 in a Harvest collection cell to a paying buyer's training run — capture, format, QA, licensing, price.
Platform AssumptionsWhy the G1 is right for the pilot, what it costs us in procurement risk, and the abstraction layer that makes every number here survive a platform change.
The Buyer UniverseNamed accounts across foundation-model labs, humanoid OEMs, funded startups and YC companies — with intake paths, budget signals and what each would actually buy.
Capacity: 100 RobotsFull-load throughput, storage volume, unit economics, and the single ratio that decides whether the fleet makes money.
Two further designs sit downstream of the operating business and are structural work rather than committed roadmap: * [**Machine Shares**](capital-structures/machine-shares) — fractional ownership of a named collection unit, with that unit's revenue distributed to holders. * [**Stake-to-Collect**](capital-structures/stake-to-collect) — an operator network where contributors post a stake against the quality of the episodes they produce. And two cross-cutting pages: the [Innovation Backlog](internal-not-for-publication/innovation-backlog) of ideas we think are genuinely new, and the [Risk Register](internal-not-for-publication/risk-register), which exists so that nobody has to discover our problems by surprise. ## How to read the numbers in this book Every financial figure here is a **model**, not a quote. Models are only as good as the assumption you disagree with least. So each one is written with its inputs visible and its sensitivity shown, and the pessimistic column is never omitted. Where a figure comes from outside research it carries its source inline. The one number to hold onto before reading anything else: > **Cost scales with hours collected. Revenue scales with hours sold. The gap between those two is the entire business.** Everything in [Unit Economics](internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics) is an elaboration of that sentence.

# Robot to Buyer: the full pipeline

## The eight stages

An episode is born, judged, packaged and licensed. Nine tenths of the operational difficulty sits in stages 4 and 5, which is where most new entrants underestimate the work.

```
1  TASK DESIGN      buyer's need  ->  a scripted, varied, gradeable task program
2  CELL SETUP       fixtures, props, lighting, camera extrinsics, calibration
3  TELEOPERATION    operator drives G1; synchronized capture at 30/100 Hz
4  INGEST + SYNC    time-align streams, segment episodes, detect dropouts
5  QA GATE          accept / reject / re-shoot; operator scorecards
6  ANNOTATION       success labels, subtask boundaries, failure causes
7  PACKAGING        GR00T LeRobot v3 conversion, stats, modality metadata
8  DELIVERY         licensed handoff + eval set retained for the buyer
```

## Stage 1 — Task design is the product

The most common failure in this business is treating a data order as a volume order. It is not. What a buyer is actually buying is **coverage of a distribution**, and the distribution is described by the task program, not by the hour count.

A weak task program: _"5,000 episodes of pick-and-place."_ A Harvest task program specifies the axes of variation and how they are sampled:

| Axis                  | Example levels for a fruit-sorting program                          |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Object identity       | apple, pear, starfruit, grape, plus 4 held-out objects              |
| Object pose           | 6 canonical, 6 adversarial (occluded, edge-of-reach, stacked)       |
| Container             | shallow basket, deep crate, divided tray                            |
| Lighting              | daylight, warm indoor, low-light, mixed/backlit                     |
| Distractors           | none / 3 / 8 non-target objects in frame                            |
| Language conditioning | 6 phrasings per task, including negations and referring expressions |
| Failure injection     | scripted drop-and-recover in 15% of episodes                        |

That last row is the one to argue for hardest in every sales conversation, because it is counterintuitive and it is where the money is. Lightwheel's Xie Chen puts it precisely: a flawless demonstration is worth **less** than one where something is dropped and recovered — _"the experience of failing then succeeding is the most valuable."_ AgiBot's open corpus makes the same design choice, retaining failed demonstrations with an explicit `error_cause` field rather than filtering them out.

Most vendors ship success-only data because success-only data is easier to QA. **Harvest ships graded failure by default, labeled, as a differentiator.** See [Innovation Backlog](../../internal-not-for-publication/innovation-backlog#failure-first-corpora).

## Stage 2 — The collection cell

The atomic operating unit is not a robot. It is a **cell**: one G1, one capture rig, one calibrated workspace, one operator seat. Cells are what we build, staff, replicate and eventually fractionalize.

A cell holds its calibration for the duration of a program. Re-calibration mid-program without re-versioning the dataset is the single most effective way to poison a corpus, because the resulting extrinsics drift is invisible in review and fatal in training.

Full specification in [The G1 Capture Stack](capture-stack).

## Stage 3 — Teleoperation

Human operators drive the robot. Control cadence and telemetry rates follow the 2026 convention that buyers' loaders expect: teleoperation command stream at 30–50 Hz, robot state telemetry at 100–200 Hz, RGB at 30 fps, gripper state at 50 Hz.

Two facts govern this stage and both are constraints, not details.

**The physical ceiling.** NVIDIA's Jim Fan states the limit bluntly: teleoperation is _"upper bounded by 24 hours per robot per day, the fundamental physical limit. And actually… it's more like three hours per robot per day."_ His three hours is a research-lab figure with no dedicated maintenance function. A disciplined commercial cell with hot-swapped batteries, a fixtured workspace and a paid technician does substantially better — our modeling runs at 6–13 collected hours per robot-day across scenarios — but the shape of his point stands. **Robot uptime is a manufactured output, not a given.** See [Capacity](../capacity/capacity).

**The operator learning curve.** Published benchmarks converge: novice operators produce 8–12 usable episodes per hour; trained operators reach 25–40 within two to three weeks. A new operator needs roughly 4–8 hours before their output is usable at all and 20–40 before it is consistently good. This is the strongest argument in the business for **retaining operators**, and the reason our staffing model treats attrition as a direct cost of goods rather than an HR metric.

## Stages 4 and 5 — Ingest and the QA gate

Raw teleoperation recordings are not training data. Between the recording and the corpus sits episode segmentation, clock alignment across streams, dropout detection, camera calibration metadata, proprioception synchronization and format conversion.

Expected rejection is **10–30%** in well-run US programs. Chinese trade reporting — the only independent full cost stack published in any language — finds 100 collected hours yielding about 50 usable, and a 12-hour collection shift producing under 6 effective hours. Our models use 65% acceptance in year one and 75–85% at maturity, and treat any month above 90% as a signal that the **QA gate is broken**, not that the operators are excellent.

One gate matters more than all the others combined: the **operator-skill calibration set**. Every operator shoots a fixed reference task before entering a program, scored against a golden reference. Programs that skip this step are reported to suffer 25–40% downstream model regression after deployment, and programs shipping 5,000+ episodes without it frequently require partial or full re-collection at 60–110% of original program cost. That is a business-ending number for a small vendor. The calibration set is non-negotiable.

## Stage 6 — Annotation

Multi-channel annotation, following the GR00T convention of `annotation.<source>.<type>`, so that a buyer can select which annotation channels to trust:

* `annotation.human.task_description` — the language instruction, in the phrasings actually used
* `annotation.human.validity` — accept/reject with reason code
* `annotation.human.subtask` — fine-grained boundaries (reach, grasp, transport, place, release)
* `annotation.human.failure_cause` — for the injected and organic failures
* `annotation.model.*` — automated pre-labels, always kept in a separate namespace from human labels

Keeping model-generated and human labels in separate namespaces is a small decision with large downstream value: it lets a buyer discount our automation without discarding our data.

## Stages 7 and 8 — Packaging and delivery

Delivery is GR00T LeRobot. Full spec in [Delivery Format and the QA Gate](delivery-format). Licensing and price in [Pricing, Licensing and Contracts](pricing-licensing).

One structural choice at delivery deserves calling out here because it compounds: **we retain a held-out evaluation split from every program and deliver it separately, on request, after the buyer's training run.**

This is not generosity. Xie Chen's most repeated observation about his own clients is that their real bottleneck is not training data at all — _"they cannot scale their evaluation anymore."_ A vendor who solves evaluation is not selling hours; a vendor selling hours is competing with a Chinese trade price and an Apache-2.0 release. Evaluation is where the relationship becomes hard to replace. See [Innovation Backlog](../../internal-not-for-publication/innovation-backlog#the-eval-wedge).

# The G1 Capture Stack

## The robot

| Attribute            | Figure                                                                       |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Height / mass        | 1.27–1.32 m, 35–47 kg depending on configuration                             |
| Degrees of freedom   | 23 base, up to 43 in EDU/Ultimate variants                                   |
| Walking speed        | up to 2 m/s                                                                  |
| Arm payload          | \~2 kg                                                                       |
| Onboard compute      | NVIDIA Jetson Orin                                                           |
| Real battery runtime | \~2 hours of _active_ use — not the 5–10 hours some marketing implies        |
| Base price           | $13,500 direct from Unitree (cut from the $16,000 launch price in late 2025) |
| EDU configurations   | quote-only from Unitree; US resellers list $43,900–$73,900                   |

**The single most important line in that table for procurement:** the $13,500 base unit **cannot be programmed** and has no SDK access. It is a demo robot. Every Harvest collection cell requires an **EDU-tier unit**, which moves the real hardware line to **$43,900 and up**. Any plan built on the $13,500 headline is a plan that does not work. Our capacity models use **$45,000 per robot**.

Battery runtime is the other figure that quietly sets throughput. Two hours of active use against a target of 9 collected hours per day means **five battery cycles per robot per shift**. Cells are specified with 6 batteries and a multi-bay charger, and battery swap is a 90-second scripted procedure, not an interruption.

## The cell

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                    │      OPERATOR STATION       │
                    │  VR HMD + hand tracking     │
                    │  or leader-arm rig          │
                    │  live multi-view monitor    │
                    └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                                   │  30–50 Hz command
                    ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
   head RGB-D ──────┤                             │
   L wrist RGB ─────┤        UNITREE G1 EDU       ├───── 100–200 Hz state
   R wrist RGB ─────┤     (Jetson Orin onboard)   │      joint pos/vel/torque
   overhead RGB ────┤                             ├───── 50 Hz gripper state
                    └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                                   │
                    ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
                    │   CAPTURE NODE (local NVMe) │
                    │  hardware-timestamped sync  │
                    │  H.264 encode + parquet     │
                    └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                                   │  nightly push
                            ┌──────▼──────┐
                            │   INGEST    │
                            └─────────────┘
```

### Sensor configuration

| Stream         | Spec                                                               | Rationale                                                                              |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Head RGB-D     | RealSense-class, 1280×720 @ 30 fps colour + 640×480 @ 30 fps depth | Matches the reference configuration NVIDIA used for its own G1 teleoperation dataset   |
| Wrist RGB ×2   | 640×480 @ 30 fps                                                   | Close-up hand-object detail is the single highest-value view for manipulation policies |
| Overhead RGB   | 1280×720 @ 30 fps                                                  | Third-person context for scene understanding and for human review during QA            |
| Proprioception | full joint position, velocity, torque @ 100 Hz                     | Goes to `observation.state`                                                            |
| Action         | commanded joint targets @ 30 Hz, aligned to frames                 | Goes to `action`                                                                       |
| Audio          | 44.1 kHz                                                           | Only for programs where verbal cues are part of the task                               |

**Hardware timestamping is mandatory.** Software-timestamped multi-camera capture drifts, and the drift is invisible until a policy trained on the data behaves badly for reasons nobody can localize. This is a cheap thing to get right at build time and an expensive thing to discover at month four.

### Teleoperation rig

Two rig families are live in the pilot, and the choice is per-program rather than global:

**VR HMD with hand tracking** — a headset plus hand/wrist tracking, retargeted to G1 joint commands via inverse kinematics. This is the reference approach: NVIDIA's own GR00T pre-training pipeline used wrist-pose trackers plus finger-tracking gloves, retargeted through IK, at a 20 Hz control cadence. Strengths: fast operator onboarding, natural for reach-and-place, works with the G1's tri-finger hands. Weakness: no force feedback.

**Leader-follower / GELLO-style kinematic leader** — a low-cost kinematic replica the operator backdrives. Strengths: far better precision on contact-rich tasks, lower operator fatigue over long shifts, cheap to replicate. Weakness: rig must be built per-embodiment, longer onboarding.

### The force-feedback problem, stated honestly

Sunday Robotics' founders make the sharpest criticism of teleoperation data that exists, and it is aimed directly at our product:

> There is no good teleoperation system that lets you feel how much force the robot is feeling. When you are teleoperating, your hand is numb.

This is true and we should not pretend otherwise. An operator without force feedback produces demonstrations with systematically wrong force profiles on contact-rich tasks — they crush or they under-grip, and they do it consistently, which means the policy learns the artifact.

Three responses, in order of how much we believe in them:

1. **Log torque anyway.** Joint torque at 100 Hz gives the buyer the true force record even when the operator could not feel it. A policy can learn from a signal the demonstrator never perceived. This is nearly free and we do it on every episode.
2. **Segment by contact-richness.** Route delicate tasks to the leader-arm rig, which transmits resistance mechanically, and reserve the VR rig for reach-and-transport programs. Charge differently for the two.
3. **Instrument the operator.** Adding force-sensing to the operator side is the real fix and it is a genuine R\&D line, not a shipping feature. Parked in the [Innovation Backlog](../../internal-not-for-publication/innovation-backlog#closing-the-force-loop).

Naming this weakness in a sales conversation before the buyer does is worth more than hiding it. Every serious buyer already knows.

## Cell bill of materials

| Line                                                      | Cost        |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| Unitree G1 EDU (tri-finger hands, SDK access)             | $45,000     |
| Cameras, mounts, capture node, NVMe, sync hardware        | $6,000      |
| Teleoperation rig (VR or leader-arm)                      | $3,000      |
| Workspace fit-out share: fixtures, lighting, props, table | $6,000      |
| **All-in per cell**                                       | **$60,000** |

This $60,000 figure is the unit that everything downstream is denominated in — it is the capex line in [Unit Economics](../internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics) and the asset behind a [Machine Share](../capital-structures/machine-shares).

# Delivery Format and the QA Gate

## Why format is a commercial decision

A buyer's cost of adopting a new data vendor is almost entirely integration cost. If our corpus loads into their existing training stack with no glue code, the evaluation is about our data. If it does not, the evaluation is about our engineering, and we lose to a vendor whose data is worse.

So the format is not a technical preference. **It is the thing that makes the first pilot cheap enough for a buyer to say yes to.**

Harvest ships **GR00T LeRobot** — standard LeRobot v2 plus the GR00T metadata extensions (`meta/modality.json`, `meta/stats.json`, and `meta/relative_stats.json`), proprioception in `observation.state`, and multi-channel annotations. This is the format NVIDIA itself publishes G1 teleoperation data in, and NVIDIA has converted major reference corpora into it (their converted BridgeData V2 corpus reports 50,415 episodes and 1,801,090 frames). Shipping into the same shape as the ecosystem's reference datasets means a buyer post-training a GR00T N-series checkpoint can point their loader at us and start.

## The layout

```
harvest-<program-id>-v<n>/
├── data/
│   └── chunk-000/
│       └── file-000.parquet          frame-level rows, many episodes per shard
├── videos/
│   ├── observation.images.head/
│   │   └── chunk-000/file-000.mp4
│   ├── observation.images.wrist_left/
│   ├── observation.images.wrist_right/
│   └── observation.images.overhead/
└── meta/
    ├── info.json                     schema, fps, codebase_version, path templates
    ├── stats.json                    global feature stats for normalization
    ├── relative_stats.json           GR00T extension
    ├── modality.json                 GR00T extension — state/action channel mapping
    ├── tasks.parquet                 language instructions -> integer task IDs
    └── episodes/
        └── chunk-000/file-000.parquet   per-episode lengths, tasks, offsets
```

Two properties of the delivery layout matter operationally. Frame rows and video frames from **many** episodes are concatenated into larger shards, with episode boundaries reconstructed from metadata offsets rather than file boundaries — which is what lets a corpus scale past a million episodes without collapsing under filesystem overhead. And `meta/info.json` is the canonical schema: features, shapes, dtypes, fps, path templates. If `info.json` is wrong, nothing else in the delivery matters.

### Parquet columns

| Column                           | Type         | Contents                                               |
| -------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `timestamp`                      | float64      | seconds from episode start                             |
| `frame_index`                    | int64        | index within episode                                   |
| `episode_index`                  | int64        | episode identifier                                     |
| `observation.state`              | list\[float] | full proprioception — joint position, velocity, torque |
| `action`                         | list\[float] | commanded joint targets, frame-aligned                 |
| `task_index`                     | int64        | resolves against `meta/tasks.parquet`                  |
| `annotation.human.validity`      | int64        | accept/reject reason code                              |
| `annotation.human.subtask`       | int64        | subtask boundary label                                 |
| `annotation.human.failure_cause` | int64        | null on clean episodes                                 |

The GR00T `modality.json` extension is what tells a training stack which slices of the `observation.state` vector correspond to which physical channel. On a 43-DOF G1 with tri-finger hands this is not optional documentation — it is the difference between a loadable dataset and a numeric blob.

## The QA gate

Every episode passes four gates in order. **Any single failure rejects the episode.** There is no partial acceptance, no "mostly fine" tier, and no manual override. An episode that cannot pass is re-shot or dropped.

### Gate 1 — Integrity (automated)

* All streams present for the full episode duration
* No frame gaps beyond one frame in any video stream
* Clock skew between streams under 10 ms at every checkpoint
* `observation.state` and `action` vectors dimensionally complete, no NaN
* Episode duration within program bounds

### Gate 2 — Kinematic sanity (automated)

* No joint commanded beyond its limit
* No velocity or acceleration discontinuity exceeding threshold (catches teleoperation dropouts that look fine on video)
* Torque profile within the envelope for the task class
* End-effector trajectory continuous — no teleports from tracking loss

### Gate 3 — Task semantics (human, sampled + model-assisted)

* Task actually attempted as specified
* Outcome label correct — success, failure, or the specific injected failure mode
* Subtask boundaries within tolerance
* Language annotation matches what was performed
* Scene matches the program's variation spec for that episode's assigned cell

Human review runs at 100% for the first 500 episodes of any program, then drops to a 15% sample plus 100% of anything an automated pre-labeller flags.

### Gate 4 — Corpus-level (per delivery)

The gate everyone forgets, and the one that protects the buyer's actual outcome. Individual episodes can all pass while the corpus is worthless.

* **Diversity audit** — coverage across every axis in the program's variation spec, with no axis level under-sampled beyond tolerance
* **Duplication audit** — near-duplicate episode detection on trajectory embeddings. This is the load-bearing one. A language-model scaling result found that repeating just **0.1% of a corpus 100 times** collapsed an 800M-parameter model's downstream performance to that of a 400M baseline. If that analogy holds even weakly in robotics, an under-varied corpus is not merely worth less — it is actively harmful to the buyer's model, and they will find out and they will not come back.
* **Operator balance** — no single operator's idiosyncratic style dominating a task class
* **Failure ratio** — injected and organic failures within the contracted band

> **Diversity and novelty, not hours, are the binding constraint.** "Hours collected" is quietly being retired as this industry's KPI. Harvest should never lead with it in a pitch, and should never be the last vendor still quoting it.

## What we report with every delivery

A delivery ships with a **corpus card** — a one-page factual record, not marketing:

1. Episode and frame counts, total collected vs. usable hours
2. Acceptance rate with rejection reasons broken out by gate
3. Diversity coverage matrix against the program's variation spec
4. Near-duplicate rate
5. Operator count and per-operator episode distribution
6. Calibration events and the episode ranges they affect
7. Held-out evaluation split: size, composition, and how to request it
8. License terms and the exact scope of rights conveyed

No competitor in this market publishes rejection reasons. Publishing ours is a strong signal precisely because it is costly to fake and slightly embarrassing to disclose.

# Pricing, Licensing and Contracts

**Last updated:** September 6, 2026

## What the market actually pays

Every figure below is vendor-reported or trade-press-reported. There is no public exchange for robot data and no neutral price index. Treat all of it as **list prices, not market quotes**.

### Per collected hour

| What is being bought                   | Reported buyer price / collected hour                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Egocentric wearable capture (no robot) | $25–60 (Chinese platforms ¥200–400, \~$29–58)                                                         |
| Single-arm teleoperation, real robot   | ¥500–1,000 (\~$72–145) in China; \~$90–150 fully loaded in the US, one published US benchmark at $118 |
| Bimanual, ALOHA-style                  | $40–80 offshore; roughly 2–4× single-arm rates onshore                                                |
| **Full humanoid, multi-sensor**        | **$80–150 per hour, or $50–150 per usable demonstration**                                             |

Harvest sells into that last row.

### The haircut nobody quotes

A collected hour is not a usable hour. With acceptance at 50–90% depending on program maturity, cost per _usable_ hour runs roughly **1.2–2×** the collected-hour figure. Finished, QA'd US teleoperation data realistically lands around **$120–200 per usable hour**.

> A per-hour quote that doesn't state throughput, geography and acceptance rate isn't a price. It's three hidden assumptions wearing a dollar sign.

### Per demonstration

Across every public source, a simple usable single-arm demonstration converges on roughly **$1–15**. Full humanoid multi-sensor demonstrations are reported at **$50–150**. The spread is explained almost entirely by how many demonstrations a vendor assumes per hour — quotes vary from 6 to 60 and rarely say which.

### The wage spread

What the people doing the work are paid, reported: Micro1 contributors around **$15/hour**; Human Archive paying Indian collectors a base rate of roughly **$1/hour** against competitors at ₹250–400 (\~$2.63–4.20); one remote egocentric posting at **$6/hour**; Tesla's own data-collection operator role at **$25–48/hour**; a current US robot-teleoperator posting at **$30–55/hour**.

That $1–15 to the worker against $25–150+ to the buyer is the spread that funds rigs, robots, QA, rejected episodes and margin. **No company discloses how it splits.** Harvest's position on this is in the [Risk Register](../../internal-not-for-publication/risk-register#labour-and-reputational-exposure), and it is a position we should take deliberately rather than by default, because it is the part of this industry most likely to become a news story.

## Harvest's price card

Three products, priced to make the first one trivially easy to buy.

### 1. Pilot Pack — fixed price, fixed scope

**$18,000 for 500 accepted episodes**, single task family, delivered in 14 days.

The point of this SKU is not margin. It is **removing the procurement decision**. $18,000 clears most engineering managers' discretionary authority without a committee, and 14 days lands inside a single training cycle. A buyer who has to run a vendor-approval process to try us will not try us.

Include in the pilot, free: the corpus card, the held-out eval split, and one re-shoot round against their feedback. The re-shoot round is the actual sales pitch — it demonstrates that we can be **directed**, which is the property a lab cannot get from an open corpus.

### 2. Program — the core business

**$110–150 per usable hour**, minimum 400 usable hours, 6–12 week delivery, priced by:

| Modifier                                                    | Effect                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Contact-rich / high-precision task class                    | +20–35%                     |
| Bimanual + full 43-DOF configuration                        | +15%                        |
| Custom environment build (kitchen, retail shelf, workbench) | fixed fee, $8–25k           |
| Exclusivity (see below)                                     | +40–100%                    |
| Failure-injection program with labelled causes              | +15% (and worth it to them) |
| Rush delivery under 21 days                                 | +25%                        |

Priced per **usable** hour, never per collected hour. This puts the acceptance risk on us, where it belongs, and it is a differentiator we should say out loud: _we don't bill you for our rejects._

### 3. Continuous Capacity — the goal

**Reserved cell-months.** A buyer reserves N cells for M months at a committed monthly rate, and directs the task program week to week.

This is the SKU the whole company should be steering toward, because it converts the fundamental problem of this business — that cost accrues on collected hours while revenue accrues on sold hours — into a solved problem. A reserved cell is sold before it collects. See [Unit Economics](../internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics), where sell-through is shown to be the variable that decides profitability.

Target: **$16,000–22,000 per cell-month** on 12-month commitments, with a task-direction SLA and a monthly diversity report.

## Licensing

Four tiers. The default is Tier 2, and the sales motion is to move accounts up.

| Tier                                          | Grant                                                                                                                                          | Price    |
| --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| **1 — Research**                              | Internal research and publication. No commercial model deployment.                                                                             | 0.6×     |
| **2 — Commercial, non-exclusive** _(default)_ | Perpetual, worldwide, irrevocable right to train and deploy commercial models. Harvest retains the right to license the same corpus to others. | 1.0×     |
| **3 — Field-exclusive**                       | Tier 2 plus exclusivity within a named application field for a defined term.                                                                   | 1.4–1.7× |
| **4 — Full exclusive / work-for-hire**        | Buyer owns the corpus outright. Harvest retains no license and no resale right.                                                                | 2.0–2.5× |

Three clauses that should appear in every Harvest agreement:

**Model outputs are unencumbered.** We claim nothing over models trained on our data. Any ambiguity here is a deal-killer at legal review and it costs us nothing to close it definitively.

**Provenance and consent warranty.** We warrant that every episode was collected by a compensated operator under contract, in a Harvest-controlled facility, with no third-party personal data captured. This is worth real money and it will be worth more. India's Ministry of Electronics and IT is already examining consent mechanisms for gig-economy physical-AI collection, and two major Indian gig platforms declined to partner with a collector over privacy concerns. **A US-controlled, facility-based, employment-contracted collection model is a compliance product, not just an operational choice.** Price it accordingly.

**Right of correction.** If a delivered corpus fails an agreed acceptance metric, we re-shoot at our cost within 30 days. Vendors who cannot offer this are signalling that they cannot control their own pipeline.

## The pricing risk, stated plainly

Prices in this market are deflating and the floor keeps being reset by free releases — Build AI's 100,405-hour Apache-2.0 corpus, AgiBot's million-plus open trajectories. XDOF's own CEO, running the best-funded pure-play data vendor, told TechCrunch that _simply creating the data itself is a poor business model_.

He is right about raw hours and wrong about the category. **Raw hours commoditize; access and curation do not.** Harvest's defensible positions are the three that survive price deflation:

1. **Direction** — a buyer can tell us what to collect next week. They cannot tell that to an Apache-2.0 release.
2. **Evaluation** — held-out, embodiment-matched eval sets against a bottleneck buyers say is worse than their data bottleneck.
3. **Provenance** — a clean, warrantable, US-facility chain of custody at a moment when the alternative is under regulatory examination.

Everything in [Pricing](#harvests-price-card) should be read as pricing those three things, with hours as the unit of account rather than the thing being sold.

# Scaling: one cell to twenty sites

## The principle

Scaling this business is not buying robots. Robots are the easy part — they arrive in four to eight weeks and they cost $45,000. **Scaling is manufacturing operator-hours and QA throughput,** and those scale on entirely different curves.

At every stage below, exactly one thing binds. Identify it, spend on it, and ignore everything else until it stops binding.

## Stage 0 — The pilot cell

**1 cell · 1–2 operators · 1 site · target: a reference corpus and a first logo**

The purpose of the pilot cell is not revenue. It is to produce **one publishable reference corpus** that a buyer can inspect before signing anything.

Concretely: replicate the structure of NVIDIA's own published G1 teleoperation dataset — 1,000 trajectories, upper-body control, language-conditioned pick-and-place with a small fixed object set, RealSense head camera, tri-finger hands — and then beat it on the axes we have chosen to compete on. Add labelled failure episodes. Add a diversity matrix. Add a held-out eval split. Publish the corpus card.

That comparison is the entire pitch, and it is legible to exactly the people we want to sell to.

**Binding constraint: our own pipeline correctness.** Nothing else matters at this stage.

## Stage 1 — The first pod

**4 cells · 8 operators · 1 site · target: 2 paying programs concurrently**

Four cells is the smallest configuration that reveals the operational truths a single cell hides: operator scheduling, battery logistics under load, QA queue depth, and the fact that two programs running concurrently contend for the same reviewer.

Introduce here, permanently:

* **Two-shift operation.** One robot, two operators, \~9 collected hours/day. Robot capex per collected hour halves. This is the single highest-leverage economic move in the entire business and it should happen as early as it can.
* **A dedicated technician.** Not a robotics engineer — a technician. Battery swaps, calibration checks, fixture resets, spares. One technician per pod protects roughly 900 collected hours a month. At any plausible rate this pays for itself several times over.
* **The QA queue as a measured system.** Queue depth in episodes, and time-to-verdict. If verdicts lag collection by more than 48 hours, operators are producing errors for two days before anyone tells them.

**Binding constraint: QA throughput.** Collection outruns review long before it outruns robots.

## Stage 2 — Site one at capacity

**20 cells · 45 operators · 1 site · target: reserved-capacity contracts**

Twenty cells is the largest single site that a single operations manager can run well, and it is where the business model should change shape. Until now we sell programs. From here we sell **reserved cell-months**.

New functions appear at this stage and each is a real hire:

* **Program manager** per major account — owns the task program, the diversity spec and the weekly re-direction conversation. This role is what buyers are actually paying the premium for.
* **Data engineer** owning the ingest, conversion and gate automation as a product with uptime, not a script.
* **Operator trainer** owning the calibration set, onboarding and the operator scorecard. Given a 4–8 hour time-to-usable and 20–40 hours to consistent quality, and given that programs skipping calibration face 25–40% downstream regression, this role is a cost-of-goods line.

**Binding constraint: operator recruitment and retention.** A trained operator is a 20–40 hour investment. Losing one is losing that investment plus the ramp of a replacement.

## Stage 3 — Multi-site

**100 cells · \~230 operators · 5 sites of 20 · target: the fleet modelled in** [**Capacity**](../capacity/capacity)

Five sites of twenty rather than one site of a hundred, for four reasons that all compound:

1. **Environmental diversity is the product.** Five geographically separate sites with genuinely different builds — a kitchen, a retail shelf run, a light-assembly bench, a warehouse pick face, a domestic living space — produce a corpus with real scene variety. One site produces a hundred cells' worth of the same room, which fails the corpus-level diversity gate no matter how good each episode is. Physical Intelligence's π0.5 generalized to unseen homes after training on roughly **100 distinct home environments** and about 400 hours of mobile-manipulation data. Environment count, not hour count, was the axis that mattered.
2. **Labour-market access.** Twenty cells is \~45 operators. Five separate markets of 45 is a far easier hiring problem than one market of 230, and it decorrelates local wage pressure.
3. **Failure isolation.** A calibration fault, a facility problem or a hardware recall hits 20 cells rather than 100.
4. **It is the natural unit for** [**Machine Shares**](../capital-structures/machine-shares)**.** A site is a coherent, auditable, revenue-attributable asset — which is exactly what a fractional instrument needs to be written against.

**Binding constraint: demand.** At 100 cells the fleet can collect far more than it can sell. This is the point where the business either has reserved-capacity contracts or it has an expensive inventory problem. Everything in [Unit Economics](../internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics) is about this transition.

## Stage 4 — The flywheel

Beyond 100 cells the honest strategic read is that pure collection stops being where value accrues. The end-state consensus across the field — Kyle Vogt, Karol Hausman, Sergey Levine — is that fleets of _working_ robots doing paid tasks eventually replace paid collection. Ken Goldberg argues the 100,000-year gap closes through engineering plus "real data flywheels," robots gathering data while doing paid work.

Harvest's version of that flywheel, in order of nearness:

1. **Evaluation-as-a-service.** Buyers say evaluation is a worse bottleneck than data. We already hold embodiment-matched eval sets and calibrated operators. This is a services line we can start selling at Stage 2 with no new capability.
2. **Human-in-the-loop rollouts.** Remote operators recover deployed robots when they fail, and the recovery _is_ the data — high-entropy, exactly at the policy's failure boundary. This is the most valuable data anyone can collect and it is generated by doing paid work rather than paying for collection.
3. **Deployed-fleet collection.** Cells doing real work in customer facilities, with data rights negotiated as part of the service contract.

Each step moves us further from selling hours and closer to owning a position that price deflation cannot reach.

## Capital at each stage

| Stage          | Cells | Cell capex | Site build | Cumulative capex |
| -------------- | ----- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------------- |
| 0 — Pilot      | 1     | $60k       | $15k       | **$75k**         |
| 1 — Pod        | 4     | $240k      | $40k       | **$280k**        |
| 2 — Site one   | 20    | $1.2M      | $180k      | **$1.38M**       |
| 3 — Multi-site | 100   | $6.0M      | $900k      | **$6.9M**        |

Cell capex is the $60,000 all-in figure from [The G1 Capture Stack](capture-stack). Site build covers facility fit-out, network, storage, and shared fixtures — it excludes working capital, which at Stage 3 is substantial because operators are paid weekly and programs invoice on delivery.

**The Stage 2 to Stage 3 jump is $5.5M of capex against unproven demand at that scale.** That is precisely the gap [Machine Shares](../capital-structures/machine-shares) exists to close, and it is the honest reason the structure is worth designing rather than a story bolted on afterwards.

# G1 Locked, Assumptions Portable

## The decision

**The Unitree G1 EDU is the pilot platform.** That is settled, and everything in [The G1 Capture Stack](../the-data-business/capture-stack) and [Capacity](../capacity/capacity) is specified against it.

The decision is genuinely well-supported:

* **It is the only capable bipedal humanoid available below $20,000** at the base tier, and the only one you can order and receive in four to eight weeks. Over 5,500 units shipped in 2025, making it the most-shipped humanoid on earth.
* **The ecosystem already speaks its language.** NVIDIA publishes a G1 teleoperation dataset — 1,000 trajectories, upper-body control, tri-finger hands, RealSense camera, language-conditioned pick-and-place. LeRobot supports it. Every buyer's stack has already met this robot.
* **The compute is the buyer's compute.** Jetson Orin onboard means our capture node and their inference target share an architecture.
* **Real deployments exist.** Japan Airlines is piloting the G1 for baggage handling at Haneda; YY Group uses it for facility cleaning; a US sheriff's department introduced one in July 2026. The platform is not a demo.
* **Institutional users include Amazon, Stanford and MIT** — which matters less technically than it does in a first sales conversation.

There is exactly one caveat and it is important enough to have its own page: see [Compliance and Procurement Risk](compliance-risk).

## Why portability is a design requirement, not a hedge

The G1 is right for the pilot. It is not obviously right for cell 100, and the honest reason is that we do not yet know what our highest-paying programs will be.

If the demand that materializes is contact-rich tabletop manipulation, a pair of static arms is a better instrument than a biped — cheaper, more reliable, higher episodes per hour, and no balance controller consuming compute and attention. If demand is mobile whole-body work, the G1 is exactly right. If it is dexterous in-hand manipulation, a specialized hand on a fixed mount beats both.

So the requirement is this:

> **Nothing in the Harvest pipeline may know what robot it is talking to, above the driver layer.**

Every model, price and process in this book is written in units that survive an embodiment change: _collected hour_, _usable hour_, _accepted episode_, _cell_, _cell-month_. None of them contain the word "G1." That is deliberate.

## The portability layer

Four boundaries. Cross them and the business becomes a G1 business rather than a data business.

### 1. The embodiment driver

One module per robot type. It exposes exactly four things upward:

```
capabilities()   -> DOF count, joint limits, sensor manifest, control rate
observe()        -> timestamped state vector + frame bundle
command(action)  -> apply commanded joint targets
calibrate()      -> extrinsics, intrinsics, joint zero, verification report
```

Everything above this line — ingest, sync, gates, annotation, packaging, delivery — is written against these four calls and nothing else. Adding a platform means writing one driver, not touching the pipeline.

### 2. The modality contract

`modality.json` already does this work in the GR00T convention: it maps slices of the state and action vectors to named physical channels. A 43-DOF G1 and a 14-DOF bimanual arm pair produce structurally identical datasets with different modality maps. **Enforce this from day one on the pilot cell, when there is only one embodiment and it feels like pointless ceremony.** It is far cheaper than retrofitting it across a live corpus.

### 3. Unit-denominated economics

Every figure in [Unit Economics](../internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics) is per collected hour, per usable hour, or per cell-month. To re-run the entire model for a different platform, three inputs change:

| Input                             | G1 EDU  | Bimanual arm cell (illustrative)       |
| --------------------------------- | ------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Robot capex                       | $45,000 | $22,000                                |
| Sustainable collected hours / day | 6–13    | 10–16 (no balance, no battery ceiling) |
| Episodes / operator-hour          | 12–40   | 20–60 (shorter cycle, fixed workspace) |

Nothing else in the model moves. That is the test of whether the abstraction is real.

### 4. Task programs are embodiment-annotated, not embodiment-specific

A task program describes a distribution — objects, poses, lighting, distractors, language, failure modes. It carries an embodiment annotation but is not written for one. This means a program sold once can be re-shot on a second platform and sold again as **cross-embodiment coverage**, which is a product buyers explicitly want: 97.6% of π0.5's first-phase training data came from robots other than the one being evaluated.

## The fleet expansion thesis

When capital allows a fleet beyond the pilot, the portability layer turns a constraint into a product. A hundred identical robots produce a hundred robots' worth of one embodiment. A hundred robots across three or four embodiments, running the _same_ task programs, produce something structurally scarcer: **matched cross-embodiment corpora**, where the task distribution is held constant and the body varies.

Almost nobody has that, because almost nobody runs more than one platform at collection scale. It is a direct answer to the cross-embodiment generalization problem that every foundation-model lab is working on, and it is a corpus that cannot be assembled after the fact from separate vendors, because the task distributions will not match.

That is worth naming as the fleet strategy rather than discovering it later: **grow by embodiment diversity at matched task programs, not by unit count at one embodiment.**

# Compliance and Procurement Risk

## Why this page exists

Harvest is a US-registered entity selling to US buyers, several of whom have federal contracts, defense-adjacent relationships or sovereign-AI commitments. Those buyers run vendor security review. If the first time we think about Unitree's regulatory posture is when a buyer's procurement team asks, we will lose the deal while we go and find out.

This page is what we say when asked. It should be accurate before it is comfortable.

## What is on the record

**DoD 1260H listing.** The US Department of Defense added Unitree to its Section 1260H list of "Chinese military companies" in **June 2026**. This is a **procurement restriction, not a purchase ban** — it constrains DoD procurement and creates reputational and contracting friction. It does not make it illegal for a private US company to buy or operate a G1.

**FCC Covered List.** A Covered List entry followed in **July 2026**. Reporting indicates the G1's FCC authorization was granted on **3 March 2025**, well before that entry, and that existing authorizations are grandfathered. Practically: units already authorized remain lawful to operate; future authorizations for new models are the exposure.

**UniPwn.** A wormable Bluetooth vulnerability disclosed in **September 2025** allows root-level takeover of affected Unitree robots within wireless range. Independent researchers have disputed the completeness of Unitree's patch, and as of the most recent reporting a full fix was not independently confirmed.

**Corporate context.** Unitree filed for a Shanghai IPO in March 2026 seeking up to $610 million. Humanoids accounted for over 51% of its revenue in 2025. This is a company under increasing public and regulatory scrutiny in both jurisdictions, which means the position above should be treated as **live, not settled**, and re-verified quarterly.

## What it actually means for Harvest

Sort the exposure by who bears it.

### It does not block the pilot

We are a private company buying a commercially available research robot to generate a dataset. No federal procurement, no defense contract, no export of controlled technology. The 1260H listing does not reach us.

### It shapes who we can sell to, and when

This is the real cost, and it is a **sales** cost, not a legal one.

| Buyer type                                         | Exposure                                                                                                   | Harvest position                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Commercial AI labs, humanoid OEMs, startups        | Low. They mostly own G1s themselves.                                                                       | Non-issue. Do not raise it unprompted.                                                                 |
| Large enterprises with federal business            | Medium. Vendor security review will surface the listing.                                                   | Lead with the isolation architecture below. Offer platform substitution.                               |
| Defense / national-security-adjacent, sovereign AI | **High.** Chinese-origin hardware in the provenance chain may be disqualifying regardless of legal status. | **Do not serve these accounts on G1-collected data.** Serve them on a non-Chinese platform or decline. |

That last row is a real revenue constraint and it should be written into the account plan rather than discovered in a late-stage review. It is also, notably, one of the strongest independent arguments for the [portability layer](../platform#the-portability-layer): a second, non-Chinese embodiment is not only a technical hedge, it unlocks a buyer segment.

### It creates a genuine security obligation

UniPwn is not a paper risk. A root-level wireless takeover of a robot in a facility with staff in it is a safety incident, not just a data-integrity one. Two safety incidents involving G1 units were reported in 2026.

**Mandatory cell network architecture:**

* **Bluetooth disabled in hardware configuration on every unit, verified at commissioning and re-verified monthly.** Not "disabled in software settings" — verified as not advertising.
* **Robots on an isolated VLAN with no route to the corporate network and no inbound internet.** Data leaves the cell by push from the capture node, never by pull from the robot.
* **Physical access control on the collection floor.** Wireless-range attacks require wireless range.
* **Firmware pinned and versioned per program.** A firmware change mid-program is a dataset-versioning event, recorded in the corpus card, exactly like a re-calibration.
* **Quarterly re-verification** of the 1260H, Covered List and CVE position, with the result written into this page and dated.

This architecture is worth building even if every Unitree concern evaporated tomorrow, because a buyer's security questionnaire will ask about it and a confident, specific answer converts.

## What we say to a buyer

Short, factual, unprompted only when the buyer's profile makes it likely to come up:

> Our pilot fleet runs Unitree G1 EDU units. Unitree was added to the DoD 1260H list in June 2026 — a procurement restriction, not a purchase ban, and it does not apply to us as a private buyer. Our units' FCC authorization predates the July 2026 Covered List entry. We run every robot Bluetooth-disabled on an isolated VLAN with no inbound route, which addresses the UniPwn class of vulnerability. Our pipeline is embodiment-agnostic above the driver layer, so if your procurement policy requires non-Chinese-origin hardware in the collection chain, we can run your program on an alternative platform. Here is what that changes in schedule and price.

The last two sentences are the ones that win. They convert a disqualification into a configuration option.

## Open items

| Item                                                                    | Status           | Owner action                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Independent confirmation of UniPwn patch status on our firmware version | **Open**         | Verify against our specific version at commissioning; do not rely on vendor claim |
| Written legal opinion on 1260H exposure for a private US data vendor    | **Not obtained** | Worth $3–5k before the first enterprise deal, not before the first startup deal   |
| Second-platform qualification (non-Chinese origin)                      | **Not started**  | Trigger at first enterprise or federal-adjacent opportunity                       |
| Insurance treatment of a robot on a Covered List                        | **Unknown**      | Raise with broker at fleet insurance binding                                      |
| Export-control review if collection ever runs outside the US            | **N/A today**    | Collection is US-only. Revisit only if that changes.                              |

Nothing on this list blocks the pilot. Every item on it blocks a specific later deal, which is why it is written down now.

  What 100 Unitree G1 cells can actually produce in a month — throughput,
  storage, and the real ceiling.
---

# 100 Robots at Full Load

**Last updated:** September 6, 2026

## The question

_If we run 100 G1 cells at capacity, how much data comes out?_

The answer has a ceiling nobody escapes and a floor set by operational discipline, and the two are a factor of three apart. Below is the full model, with the assumptions exposed so each can be argued with individually.

## The physical ceiling

Start with the hard limit. Jim Fan states it as directly as it can be stated:

> Teleoperation is upper bounded by 24 hours per robot per day, the fundamental physical limit. And actually, it's more like three hours per robot per day.

His three hours is a research-lab number — shared robots, no dedicated maintenance, graduate-student scheduling. A commercial cell does better, but the ceiling is real and it is set by four things:

| Constraint                             | Effect on collected hours/day                                                                              |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Battery** — \~2 hours active runtime | 5 swap cycles for a 9-hour day. Solved with 6 batteries + multi-bay charger + 90-second scripted swap      |
| **Operator fatigue**                   | Teleoperation is cognitively heavy. \~4.5 productive hours per operator-shift, so two shifts per robot-day |
| **Reset and fixture time**             | 15–25% of wall-clock. Attacked with fixtured workspaces and scripted resets, never eliminated              |
| **Maintenance and calibration**        | \~5% of wall-clock in steady state, higher during ramp                                                     |

**Absolute theoretical ceiling: \~16 collected hours per robot-day** at three shifts with perfect logistics. **Sustainable planning ceiling: 13.** **Realistic base case: 9.**

## Throughput scenarios

Three scenarios. Every input is stated; disagree with them individually rather than with the totals.

| Input                         | Conservative | Base | Stretch |
| ----------------------------- | ------------ | ---- | ------- |
| Collected hours / robot / day | 6.0          | 9.0  | 13.0    |
| Collection days / month       | 24           | 26   | 26      |
| QA acceptance rate            | 65%          | 75%  | 85%     |
| Episodes / operator-hour      | 12           | 25   | 40      |

### Output at 100 cells

| Output                            | Conservative | Base    | Stretch   |
| --------------------------------- | ------------ | ------- | --------- |
| **Collected robot-hours / month** | 14,400       | 23,400  | 33,800    |
| **Usable hours / month**          | 9,360        | 17,550  | 28,730    |
| **Accepted episodes / month**     | 112,320      | 438,750 | 1,149,200 |
| **Usable hours / year**           | 112,320      | 210,600 | 344,760   |

### Reading these numbers against the field

**They are large.** Base case annual output of **210,600 usable hours** exceeds Generalist's entire GEN-0 training corpus of 270,000 hours in about fifteen months, and comfortably exceeds Ant Lingbo's stated 60,000-hour corpus within four months. Scale AI reported delivering 150,000+ hours of physical-AI data across all of 2025; our base case passes that annually.

**And they are small.** Generalist claims collection above **10,000 hours per week**. Our base case month is roughly two days of their intake. Shen Yujun's "robot GPT-1 moment" threshold of 1,000,000 hours would take our base-case fleet **57 years**.

Both readings are correct and together they define the strategy:

> **We cannot win on volume and we do not need to. A hundred cells is enough to be a serious, differentiated supplier of directed, high-quality, embodiment-matched data. It is not enough to be an undifferentiated hours vendor, and attempting that is the failure mode.**

## Episode counts and the honest caveat

The episode figures above — up to 1.1M/month in the stretch case — are arithmetically correct and commercially misleading, because episodes-per-hour is not a productivity metric. It is a **task-length** metric.

40 episodes/hour means 90-second episodes. That is a short pick-and-place. A contact-rich assembly task runs 3–8 minutes and yields 8–20 episodes/hour. A long-horizon mobile manipulation task might yield 4.

So a vendor advertising a large episode count is, more often than not, advertising short tasks. **Harvest quotes hours and task-class, and treats any episode-count comparison as a question about task length until proven otherwise.** This is worth being explicit about in sales conversations, because it reframes a comparison we would otherwise lose.

## Storage and data volume

Storage is a real cost line at fleet scale and it is set by the sensor tier the program specifies.

### Per collected robot-hour

| Tier  | Configuration                                     | GB / collected hour |
| ----- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| **A** | 3× RGB 720p30 @ 5 Mbps + full proprioception      | **7.0 GB**          |
| **B** | 3× RGB 1080p30 @ 8 Mbps + full proprioception     | **11.1 GB**         |
| **C** | Tier B + depth 640×480 @ 30 fps (5:1 compression) | **24.4 GB**         |

Proprioception — 43 DOF at position, velocity and torque, 100 Hz — is about **0.29 GB per hour**. It is the most valuable data we produce and it is 1–4% of the bytes. Video dominates entirely, which means every storage decision is a video decision.

### Monthly fleet volume, 100 cells

| Scenario     | Tier A     | Tier B     | Tier C     |
| ------------ | ---------- | ---------- | ---------- |
| Conservative | 101 TB     | 160 TB     | 351 TB     |
| **Base**     | **165 TB** | **260 TB** | **570 TB** |
| Stretch      | 238 TB     | 375 TB     | 823 TB     |

Base case at Tier B: **260 TB/month, 3.1 PB/year** of raw collected data. After rejecting 25% at the QA gate, roughly **195 TB/month** enters the delivered corpus.

**Depth is the decision.** Tier C is 2.2× the storage of Tier B for a modality many manipulation policies do not consume. Default to Tier B; enable depth per-program when the buyer asks for it and price the storage into that program. Recording depth at 15 Hz rather than 30 halves the cost with minimal information loss for most manipulation tasks.

### Storage architecture

* **Hot (0–30 days)** — full raw, on fast object storage, pending QA and delivery
* **Warm (1–12 months)** — accepted episodes only, for re-licensing and cross-program assembly
* **Cold (12 months+)** — accepted episodes in archival storage; rejected episodes deleted after 90 days except a sampled set retained for QA-model training
* **Egress** is the surprise line. A 400-hour program delivery at Tier B is \~4.4 TB moving to a buyer. Negotiate egress terms before signing the first large program, not after.

## The real ceiling

The physical ceiling is 16 collected hours per robot-day. **The binding ceiling is demand.**

At 100 cells in the base case we produce 17,550 usable hours a month. Selling that at $110/hour requires roughly **$1.9M of monthly recurring demand** — in a market whose only public estimate is low hundreds of millions annually. It is achievable, and it is not automatic, and it will not happen through inbound.

This is why [reserved capacity](../../the-data-business/pricing-licensing#3-continuous-capacity--the-goal) is the strategic priority and not a pricing footnote, and why the next page is the most important one in this book.

# Agent Architecture Overview

Harvest's core constraint isn't demand — it's throughput per dollar of headcount. Every stage in [Robot to Buyer: the full pipeline](../the-data-business/data-business) — scheduling a cell, QA-gating an episode, matching a buyer to available capacity, pricing a deal, watching for a stuck operator — is a decision that today takes a person's attention. The thesis of this section is that most of those decisions are narrow, repeatable, and auditable enough to hand to an agent, which is the only way the [Scaling: one cell to twenty sites](../the-data-business/scaling) trajectory works without headcount scaling linearly with cell count.

This page is the map. The rest of the section covers the framework for what agents are allowed to decide alone ([Autonomous Decision-Making Framework](autonomous-decision-making)), how multiple agents divide the work and hand off to each other ([Multi-Agent Orchestration & Roles](agent-orchestration)), where a human has to be in the loop and why ([Human-in-the-Loop vs Full Autonomy](human-in-the-loop)), and how this compounds into the scaling story ([Scaling the Business with Agents](scaling-with-agents)).

### Why agents, specifically, and not just "more software"

Two things distinguish an agent from a conventional automation script here: it makes a judgment call from an underspecified input (an episode that's ambiguous, not cleanly pass/fail; a buyer inquiry that doesn't match a template), and it can chain multiple tool calls to resolve that judgment call — pull the episode's sensor traces, compare against a reference success pattern, flag or clear it, log the reasoning. A fixed-rule QA script can't do that; a person reviewing every episode by hand doesn't scale past a handful of cells. The agent layer sits in between.

### The five agent roles

| Agent                           | Sits between                             | Primary job                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Capture QA Agent**            | Raw session → annotated episode          | Runs the QA gate from [Delivery Format and the QA Gate](../the-data-business/delivery-format): validates modality completeness, flags failed/ambiguous episodes, routes edge cases to a human reviewer.                                                                                          |
| **Scheduling & Capacity Agent** | Operator availability → cell utilization | Assigns task programs to open cells and operators to maximize the sell-through ratio modeled in [Unit Economics and Break-even](../internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics).                                                                                                                 |
| **Buyer-Matching Agent**        | Inbound inquiry → qualified lead         | Screens inbound interest against the profiles in [The Buyer Universe](../internal-not-for-publication/buyers) and [Target Account List](../internal-not-for-publication/target-list), and drafts a first-touch response per [Outreach Playbook](../internal-not-for-publication/outreach).       |
| **Pricing & Contract Agent**    | Qualified lead → Order Form              | Assembles a proposed Order Form against the tiering in [Pricing, Licensing and Contracts](../the-data-business/pricing-licensing), within pre-authorized bounds (see [Autonomous Decision-Making Framework](autonomous-decision-making)).                                                        |
| **Compliance Screening Agent**  | Any new counterparty → cleared/blocked   | Runs the denied-party and entity-list screening required by [Export Control & Compliance](../legal-and-corporate/export-control) before any dataset access is granted — this one is deliberately narrow and never fully autonomous; see [Human-in-the-Loop vs Full Autonomy](human-in-the-loop). |

### Design principle: narrow scope, wide logging

Every agent in this stack has one clearly-bounded decision type, not a general mandate. This is a deliberate rejection of a single "ops agent that does everything" — a narrow agent is auditable (you can review 100% of its decisions against a fixed rubric), replaceable (swapping the QA agent's model doesn't touch the pricing agent), and safe to expand incrementally (a new agent role gets added when a decision type becomes repeatable enough to specify, not before). Every agent action — not just its output — is logged with the reasoning trace and the tool calls it made, both for the audit trail required in [Human-in-the-Loop vs Full Autonomy](human-in-the-loop) and because that log is itself a QA signal on the agent's own performance.

### What's explicitly not automated

Operator safety decisions, anything touching an operator's consent or compensation under the [Operator Agreement](../legal-and-corporate/operator-agreement), and any counterparty screening result under [Export Control & Compliance](../legal-and-corporate/export-control) always route to a human. This isn't a temporary limitation — it's the permanent boundary described in [Human-in-the-Loop vs Full Autonomy](human-in-the-loop).

# Autonomous Decision-Making Framework

The question every agent role in [Agent Architecture Overview](ai-agents) has to answer before it ships is not "can the model do this?" but "what happens the day it's wrong?" This page is the framework for answering that, and the actual authority boundaries for each of the five agents.

### The three tiers

**Tier 1 — Fully autonomous.** The agent decides and acts with no human in the approval path. Reserved for decisions that are high-frequency, cheaply reversible, and where a wrong call has a bounded, recoverable cost.

**Tier 2 — Autonomous within pre-authorized bounds, human notified.** The agent decides and acts, but only within limits a human set in advance (a price floor, a discount cap, an episode-count threshold), and every action is logged to a review queue a human clears asynchronously — the human isn't blocking the decision, but is checking it after the fact on a fixed cadence.

**Tier 3 — Agent recommends, human decides.** The agent does the analysis and drafts the action, but nothing executes without an explicit human approval. Reserved for anything irreversible, high-cost, or touching a legal or safety boundary.

### Authority table by agent

| Agent                 | Tier 1 (auto)                                                                                | Tier 2 (bounded, logged)                                                                                                                     | Tier 3 (recommend only)                                                                                 |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Capture QA            | Clear an episode that passes every modality/completeness check with no ambiguity flags       | Route a borderline episode to the reviewer queue with a specific flagged reason                                                              | Discard an episode outright (destructive; always reviewed first)                                        |
| Scheduling & Capacity | Assign a routine task program to an open cell/operator pairing                               | Rebalance the week's schedule to protect the sell-through ratio, within the ±15% capacity-shift band a human set                             | Add or remove a cell from rotation entirely                                                             |
| Buyer-Matching        | Send an auto-reply acknowledging inbound interest and requesting standard qualification info | Route a qualified lead to the pipeline with a suggested tier from [Pricing, Licensing and Contracts](../the-data-business/pricing-licensing) | Represent Harvest's capacity, exclusivity availability, or timeline to a buyer without a human sign-off |
| Pricing & Contract    | Generate a draft Order Form at list price for a standard, non-exclusive tier                 | Offer a discount up to the pre-authorized band (e.g., 10%) for a qualified repeat buyer                                                      | Offer exclusivity, a custom tier, or any discount beyond the pre-authorized band                        |
| Compliance Screening  | Run the denied-party/entity-list check and log a clean result                                | — (no bounded-autonomy tier for this agent — see below)                                                                                      | Any flagged or ambiguous screening result always escalates; the agent never clears a flag itself        |

The Compliance Screening Agent is the one deliberate exception to the three-tier pattern: it has a Tier 1 action (run the check, log a clean pass) and a Tier 3 escalation (anything else), but no Tier 2. There is no version of "proceed with a flagged counterparty, notify a human after" that is acceptable given the exposure in [Export Control & Compliance](../legal-and-corporate/export-control).

### What moves a decision up a tier

A decision starts in the lowest tier the risk analysis supports and only moves to full autonomy after a track record — specifically: (1) a minimum sample size of human-reviewed Tier 3/2 decisions, (2) an agreement rate against human judgment above a set threshold measured over that sample, and (3) no unresolved disagreement on a high-cost case. This mirrors the QA-gate philosophy in [Delivery Format and the QA Gate](../the-data-business/delivery-format) — trust is earned by measured track record, not granted by default.

### What happens when an agent is wrong

Every Tier 1 and Tier 2 action is reversible by design or bounded in blast radius: a wrongly-cleared borderline episode is caught by the buyer's own acceptance-review window in the [Data License Agreement](../legal-and-corporate/data-license-agreement); a wrongly-scheduled cell loses a few hours of throughput, not a buyer relationship. Tier 3's entire purpose is to keep the genuinely unbounded-cost decisions — an exclusivity commitment, a discard, a compliance clearance — behind a human regardless of how good the agent gets. This is a permanent design choice, not a maturity stage the business grows out of; see [Human-in-the-Loop vs Full Autonomy](human-in-the-loop) for why.

### Kill switch

Any agent's autonomous authority (Tier 1 and Tier 2) can be revoked instantly and independently of the others — by role, not globally — if its logged decision quality degrades, a buyer disputes a decision it made, or the underlying model or tool it depends on changes. Reverting an agent to full Tier 3 (recommend-only) never requires a deployment change, only a config flag, by design.
