# Multi-Agent Orchestration & Roles

The five agents in [Agent Architecture Overview](ai-agents) don't run in isolation — an episode has to pass through QA before it can be scheduled for delivery, a buyer match has to clear compliance screening before pricing drafts a contract. This page is how they hand off to each other, and the failure modes that come specifically from chaining agents rather than running one.

### The handoff graph

```
Session recorded (cell) 
        │
        ▼
  Capture QA Agent ──fails/ambiguous──► Human reviewer queue
        │ passes
        ▼
  Episode enters licensable pool
        │
        ▼
Buyer-Matching Agent ◄── inbound inquiry
        │ qualified lead
        ▼
Compliance Screening Agent ──flagged──► Human (Tier 3, always)
        │ cleared
        ▼
  Pricing & Contract Agent ──beyond band──► Human (Tier 3)
        │ within band
        ▼
   Draft Order Form → human countersignature (contracts are never auto-executed)

Scheduling & Capacity Agent runs continuously alongside this chain,
consuming the licensable-pool growth rate and operator availability
to keep the sell-through ratio on target.
```

### Orchestration pattern: sequential handoff, not a shared brain

Each agent owns its stage and passes a structured result forward — not a shared context window, not one model doing everything with different prompts. This is the same narrow-scope principle from [Agent Architecture Overview](ai-agents) applied at the system level: the Buyer-Matching Agent doesn't need to know how QA scored an episode, only that the licensable pool has capacity in a given task category; the Pricing Agent doesn't need session-level detail, only the qualified lead and tier. This keeps each agent's context small (cheaper, faster, less prone to the kind of error that comes from an overloaded prompt) and keeps the failure surface local — a bad Pricing Agent output can't corrupt QA's judgment, because it never sees QA's raw reasoning, only its verdict.

### Where compliance sits in the chain, deliberately

Compliance Screening runs after Buyer-Matching but before Pricing — never after. A counterparty is screened before Harvest spends any effort drafting terms for them, which matters operationally (don't do contract work for a party you can't legally sell to) and matters as a hard architectural guarantee: there is no path through this graph where a priced Order Form reaches a human for signature without a compliance clearance already logged against it. That ordering is enforced in the orchestration layer itself, not left to agent judgment.

### Failure modes specific to chaining

**Cascade errors.** If the QA Agent mis-clears a borderline episode, that error can propagate into a licensed dataset before a human ever sees it. Mitigation: QA's Tier 1 threshold (see [Autonomous Decision-Making Framework](autonomous-decision-making)) is set conservatively, and the buyer's own acceptance-review window under the [Data License Agreement](../legal-and-corporate/data-license-agreement) is the backstop, not the only line of defense.

**Stale handoff state.** The Scheduling Agent optimizing against a licensable-pool figure that Buyer-Matching hasn't updated yet leads to over- or under-booking. Mitigation: every agent reads from a single source-of-truth state store rather than each other's outputs directly, and every write is timestamped so a downstream agent can detect stale input and pause rather than act on it.

**Silent disagreement.** Two agents making individually reasonable but mutually inconsistent calls (Pricing offers a discount tier that Scheduling can't actually deliver capacity for). Mitigation: the Order Form draft step cross-checks against live Scheduling Agent capacity output before it's presented for human countersignature — this is the one place two agents' outputs are deliberately reconciled before a human sees the result, rather than left for the human to catch.

### Observability

Every handoff in the graph above is logged with the input state, the decision, the tier it was made under, and — for anything routed to a human — the reason. This log is the same one referenced in [Agent Architecture Overview](ai-agents) and is what makes the tier-promotion process in [Autonomous Decision-Making Framework](autonomous-decision-making) possible: without a full trace of every handoff, there's no way to measure an agent's real agreement rate against human judgment.

pages.title: Human-in-the-Loop vs Full Autonomy
pages.markdown:
# Human-in-the-Loop vs Full Autonomy

Every agent business eventually gets asked the same question by a buyer's diligence team, an insurer, or an investor: _what's actually automated, and what happens when it's wrong?_ This page is the direct answer, and the governance structure behind it.

### The permanent boundary

Three categories never move to full autonomy, regardless of track record, and this is a policy decision, not a capability gap that better models will eventually close:

1. **Operator safety.** No agent has authority to modify a collection cell's safety configuration, override an emergency stop, or direct an operator into a task the safety briefing under Section 5 of the [Operator Agreement](../legal-and-corporate/operator-agreement) hasn't covered.
2. **Consent and compensation.** No agent has authority to alter what an operator has consented to under Section 4 of the [Operator Agreement](../legal-and-corporate/operator-agreement), or to change compensation terms.
3. **Compliance clearance.** No agent has authority to clear a flagged counterparty under [Export Control & Compliance](../legal-and-corporate/export-control). The Compliance Screening Agent, per [Multi-Agent Orchestration & Roles](agent-orchestration), can only escalate — never clear — a flag.

Everything else is a question of tier, addressed in [Autonomous Decision-Making Framework](autonomous-decision-making), and tiers can move as track record accumulates.

### Why this line is drawn here specifically

The three categories above share a property the rest of the pipeline doesn't: the cost of a wrong autonomous decision is not fully recoverable by a downstream check. A mispriced Order Form gets caught at contract signature; a mis-cleared episode gets caught at the buyer's acceptance window. An operator safety incident, a consent violation, or an export control breach doesn't have an equivalent downstream catch — by the time it's visible, the harm (physical, legal, or reputational) has already happened. That asymmetry, not a general discomfort with autonomy, is the actual reasoning, and it's worth stating plainly because it's the answer to give a buyer's or insurer's diligence question directly.

### Governance structure

* **Review cadence.** Tier 2 (bounded-autonomy) decisions are reviewed on a fixed weekly cadence per agent, not on demand — this keeps review from silently lapsing under operational pressure.
* **Escalation ownership.** Every Tier 3 recommendation has a named human owner responsible for the decision, not a general queue anyone can pick up — accountability for an agent's recommendation sits with a specific person the same way it would for a report from a junior analyst.
* **Incident response.** Any operator safety event, consent dispute, or compliance flag triggers the same incident process regardless of whether an agent was involved in the chain that led to it — agents don't get a separate, lighter-touch incident process just because software was involved.
* **Audit trail.** The full decision log described in [Multi-Agent Orchestration & Roles](agent-orchestration) is retained for the same period as the compliance records required under [Export Control & Compliance](../legal-and-corporate/export-control), and is the first artifact produced in response to a buyer's security/diligence questionnaire or a regulator's inquiry.

### What this buys the business

A buyer, insurer, or investor evaluating Harvest can be shown exactly which decisions are automated, exactly which are not, and exactly why the line is where it is — not as a compliance afterthought, but as the actual design. That answer is a commercial asset: it's the difference between "we use AI to move fast" (a claim every competitor makes) and a governance structure specific enough to survive a real diligence process.

# Scaling the Business with Agents

[Scaling: one cell to twenty sites](../the-data-business/scaling) lays out the staged path in terms of cells and sites. This page lays out the same path in terms of what has to be true of the agent layer at each stage for headcount not to scale linearly with it — which is the actual point of everything in this section.

### The headcount problem this solves

A collection operation run entirely by humans scales operations headcount roughly linearly with cell count: more cells means more QA reviewers, more schedulers, more people fielding buyer inquiries. That ratio is what caps how fast a data-collection business can grow without either raising a lot more capital than the unit economics in [Unit Economics and Break-even](../internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics) can support, or growing slowly. The agent layer's entire commercial justification is bending that curve — not eliminating people, but making the ratio of ops headcount to cell count fall as cell count rises.

### Stage-by-stage agent maturity

**Stage 1 — Single pilot cell (current).** Every agent role exists but runs mostly in Tier 3 (recommend-only) per [Autonomous Decision-Making Framework](autonomous-decision-making) — the track record needed to earn Tier 1/2 authority doesn't exist yet at this volume. Human review is the actual bottleneck and that's expected: this stage is where the review data that justifies later autonomy gets generated.

**Stage 2 — Multi-cell, single site (5–10 cells).** Capture QA and Scheduling agents cross the sample-size threshold first, because they run at session frequency, not deal frequency — they earn Tier 1/2 authority fastest. This is the stage where a single ops person can plausibly run a full site, because the two highest-frequency decision types are now substantially automated.

**Stage 3 — Multi-site (per** [**Scaling: one cell to twenty sites**](../the-data-business/scaling)**).** Buyer-Matching and Pricing agents earn Tier 2 authority as deal volume accumulates enough track record. This is the stage where the agent layer starts doing genuinely novel work beyond replicating what a human would do per-site: the Scheduling Agent is now optimizing capacity allocation _across_ sites, routing a buyer's task-category demand to whichever site has open capacity — a coordination problem that doesn't have a clean single-human owner even in the fully-staffed alternative.

**Stage 4 — National multi-site network.** The constraint shifts from "can an agent make this decision" to "does the orchestration graph in [Multi-Agent Orchestration & Roles](agent-orchestration) hold up under volume" — this is a systems and observability problem more than a model-capability one, and it's the stage at which the audit trail and incident-response discipline from [Human-in-the-Loop vs Full Autonomy](human-in-the-loop) stops being good practice and starts being operationally load-bearing.

### What doesn't scale with agents, on purpose

Physical cell setup, operator hiring and safety training, and site-lease negotiation stay human end to end at every stage — these aren't decision-automation problems, they're physical-world and relationship problems the agent layer was never designed to touch. The [Compliance Screening Agent](ai-agents)'s Tier 3-only design (see [Autonomous Decision-Making Framework](autonomous-decision-making)) means compliance headcount scales with counterparty _volume_ even as it doesn't scale with cell count — a deliberate trade that keeps the one irreducibly-human check from becoming the growth bottleneck it would be if under-resourced.

### The honest limit

This model compounds the throughput side of the business — more cells, more deals, more episodes reviewed per hour of human attention — but it does not compound the physical side. The number of Unitree G1 units Harvest can lease, staff, and safely operate is still bound by capital and hiring, not by agent capability. Reading this page as "agents let Harvest scale infinitely" would be the wrong takeaway; the honest claim is narrower and still real: agents let the _operations_ function scale sub-linearly with cell count, which changes the unit economics in [Unit Economics and Break-even](../internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics) materially, but doesn't change the physical constraint the [Risk Register](../internal-not-for-publication/risk-register) already tracks.

# Machine Shares: Fractional Robot Ownership

> **Status: design document.** This describes a structure Harvest could build. It is not an offer, a solicitation, or a commitment to build it. Nothing here is investment advice, and no instrument described here should be offered to anyone before securities counsel has reviewed the specific structure, the specific jurisdiction and the specific marketing language.

## Why this structure exists

The [scaling plan](../../the-data-business/scaling#capital-at-each-stage) needs **$6.9M** to go from a proven 20-cell site to a 100-cell multi-site fleet. That capital is buying depreciating physical assets with contracted or near-contracted revenue against them — which is the wrong shape for equity venture capital and the right shape for asset finance.

A venture round prices the whole company's future. Asset finance prices a machine. When you know what the machine costs, what it produces and what that output sells for, you should be financing the machine.

The three genuine advantages of doing it as fractional machine shares rather than a bank facility:

**The asset is legible.** A collection cell is a $60,000 physical object at a known address with a serial number, a measurable output in hours and episodes, and revenue attributable to it by contract. That is more auditable than almost anything in real-estate tokenization, which is the sector that pioneered this structure.

**The revenue is attributable without allocation games.** Cell #47's episodes carry cell #47's identifier through the pipeline into the delivery manifest. Revenue attribution is a database join, not a management judgement. This is unusual and it is the strongest single argument for the structure.

**The buyer base is aligned.** The people most likely to want exposure to physical AI are the people least able to access it — the sector's private rounds are closed to them. A $500 position in a real robot generating real revenue is a genuinely differentiated product, and it is why comparable structures exist: XMAQUINA runs a machine-RWA DAO on peaq with a reported \~$28M treasury as of May 2026, and has partnered with tokenization platforms specifically to fractionalize autonomous machines.

## The unit

Everything is denominated in a **Collection Unit**: one G1 EDU, one capture rig, one calibrated workspace, one site allocation.

|                                |                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| All-in cost                    | **$60,000** _(see_ [_Capture Stack_](../../the-data-business/capture-stack#cell-bill-of-materials)_)_ |
| Design life                    | 36 months, depreciated over 24                                                                        |
| Base-case output               | 200 collected hours/month → 150 usable hours                                                          |
| Base-case attributable revenue | $10,725/month at 65% sell-through, $110/usable hour                                                   |
| Base-case unit EBITDA          | $3,015/month                                                                                          |

## Structure

Three layers. Each does exactly one job, and the separation is what makes the thing auditable.

```
   ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  HARVEST OPERATING CO.  (Delaware)                │
   │  employs operators · holds buyer contracts        │
   │  runs QA, pipeline, sales · owns the brand        │
   └────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                        │  Master Services Agreement
                        │  (operator fee + revenue share)
   ┌────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
   │  HARVEST FLEET I, LLC   (Series LLC or SPV)       │
   │  OWNS the robots and capture rigs                 │
   │  Series A = Site 1 cells 1–20                     │
   │  Series B = Site 2 cells 21–40    ...             │
   └────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                        │  Membership interests
   ┌────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
   │  HOLDERS                                          │
   │  fractional interests in a named Series           │
   │  entitled to that Series' distributable cash      │
   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Why a Series LLC.** Each Series is a segregated pool with its own assets, its own revenue and its own liabilities. A holder in Series B has no exposure to Series A's performance. This is the standard structure for fractional aircraft, equipment leasing and collectible platforms, and it is well understood by counsel, administrators and auditors — which matters more than elegance.

**Why the operator is separate from the owner.** OpCo takes operational risk — employment, contracts, sales, liability. FleetCo takes asset risk. A holder is exposed to the machine's economics, not to a lawsuit against the operating business. This separation is also what makes the revenue attribution auditable: the MSA specifies exactly how revenue is assigned to a Series, and an auditor can check it.

**The Series is a site, not a single robot.** This is the most important structural choice on this page, and it is the one that will be argued about.

A single named robot is the more emotionally compelling product — _you own Robot 47_ — and it is operationally worse in three ways that all bite. One robot's revenue is lumpy: a two-week hardware fault takes a holder's distributions to zero. One robot cannot be re-tasked without touching the asset a holder thinks they own. And a hundred single-robot Series is a hundred sets of accounts, filings and distributions, which is an administrative cost that eats the yield it is meant to deliver.

A 20-cell Series diversifies hardware faults, smooths utilization, and costs one twentieth as much to administer. **Sell the site, name the robots.** Holders get a named-robot dashboard — serial number, uptime, hours collected, episodes accepted, revenue contributed — without owning a single point of failure. All of the emotional product, none of the operational fragility.

## What holders get

**A pro-rata claim on Series distributable cash**, defined precisely, in this order:

1. Attributable revenue: gross revenue from programs, allocated by the delivered hours each cell in the Series contributed
2. Less operator fee to OpCo: a fixed per-cell-month fee covering operators, QA, site and infrastructure
3. Less maintenance reserve: a fixed monthly accrual, with any surplus released at Series wind-up
4. Less asset-level insurance and Series administration
5. \= **Series Distributable Cash**, split by an agreed waterfall between holders and OpCo

Distributions quarterly. Not monthly — monthly distributions on a business with lumpy program revenue force either a cash buffer that depresses yield or a distribution that is sometimes zero, and neither is a good holder experience.

**Reporting** — and this is where the structure earns trust or loses it:

* Monthly: per-cell uptime, collected hours, accepted episodes, acceptance rate, sell-through
* Quarterly: Series financials, distribution calculation with the arithmetic shown, maintenance reserve position
* Annually: independent review of revenue attribution against delivery manifests

**What holders do not get:** control over task programs, buyer selection, pricing or operations. Those sit with OpCo, and the separation is deliberate. A holder base that can vote on operations is a holder base that will vote to maximize this quarter's distribution at the expense of the asset — and it materially strengthens the argument that they are relying on someone else's efforts, which is the exact thing that determines the security analysis in [Regulatory Pathways](../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield).

## Why the yield story is clean

Compared with almost anything else marketed as a real-world asset:

| Property                                   | Harvest Collection Unit                           | Typical RWA offering                   |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Asset exists physically                    | Yes, at a known address, serialized               | Often                                  |
| Revenue directly attributable to the asset | Yes, by delivery manifest join                    | Rarely — usually pool-level allocation |
| Revenue independently verifiable           | Yes, against buyer contracts and delivery records | Rarely                                 |
| Operating costs known and stable           | Yes, dominated by wages                           | Often opaque                           |
| Asset has residual value                   | Yes — G1 EDU has an active secondary market       | Sometimes                              |
| Depends on token price                     | **No**                                            | Frequently                             |

That last row is the whole argument. **The unit generates dollars from enterprise buyers under contract.** If a token layer is ever added, it is a settlement and transfer mechanism, not the source of yield. Any structure whose returns depend on token appreciation is a different product with a different risk profile, and conflating the two is how this category has repeatedly damaged itself.

## Why it might not work

Three failure modes, stated before anyone else states them.

**Sell-through.** Per [Unit Economics](../../internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics#sell-through-the-number-that-actually-matters), a unit below roughly 55% sell-through does not cover its costs. A holder in a Series that has not sold its capacity receives nothing, and can face a maintenance-reserve call. **No Series should be offered before its cells are covered by contracted or reserved demand.** Financing capacity ahead of demand is how this structure becomes a liability for both sides.

**Depreciation is real and fast.** These are 24-month assets in a market where the hardware is getting cheaper and better every year. A holder's capital is being returned through distributions, not preserved in the asset. Any presentation that shows a yield without showing the depreciation curve alongside it is misleading, and the offering documents must show both.

**It is very likely a security.** See [Regulatory Pathways](../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield). This is not a reason not to do it. It is a reason to do it through a compliant exemption from the beginning, which is entirely achievable and much cheaper than fixing it afterwards.

# Investor Guide: From Interest to Holding

[Machine Shares](machine-shares) and [Regulatory Pathways](../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield) describe the structure and the legal routes. This page describes the experience — what a holder actually does, receives, and should expect, walked through in order. Nothing here is an offer; it describes a process Harvest would run once a specific Series is open under a specific exemption with counsel-approved documents.

## Step 1 — Which route applies to you

The route determines everything downstream: who can invest, how much, and through what channel. Per [Regulatory Pathways](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-four-routes):

| If you are...                                                                      | The route     | Ticket size                                                    | Where                              |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| An accredited investor (income >$200K/$300K joint, or $1M+ net worth ex-residence) | Reg D 506(c)  | No regulatory cap; Harvest sets a practical minimum per Series | Direct, off a public offering page |
| Not accredited, income or net worth under $124,000                                 | Reg CF        | Greater of $2,500 or 5% of the greater of income/net worth     | A single registered funding portal |
| Not accredited, income and net worth both at or above $124,000                     | Reg CF        | 10% of the greater, capped at $124,000                         | A single registered funding portal |
| Anyone, once a Series has scaled to a Reg A+ offering                              | Reg A+ Tier 2 | Non-accredited capped at 10% of income/net worth               | Direct or through a broker-dealer  |

**Series A launches under Reg D 506(c) first**, per [the recommendation](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#recommendation) — so the first cohort of holders will be accredited investors, verified. A Reg CF community round follows once a Series has a real distribution track record to show, not before.

## Step 2 — Verification, before you see a subscription document

**Accredited status (Reg D).** General solicitation under 506(c) requires _verified_ accreditation, not a self-certification checkbox — this is the one meaningful extra step relative to older 506(b) deals. Verification runs through a third-party service against one of: income documentation (W-2s, tax returns, or a letter from a CPA/attorney), net-worth documentation (bank/brokerage statements plus a credit report for liabilities), or a professional-license path (Series 7/65/82 holders). Cost is typically a few hundred dollars, generally covered by the platform or the offering, not billed to the investor as a separate line item.

**Identity and AML (all routes).** Standard KYC — government ID, address verification, sanctions and PEP screening — run through the transfer agent or funding portal, not by Harvest directly. This happens once per investor per platform, not once per Series.

**Reg CF investor-limit self-certification.** Reg CF's per-investor caps are calculated from income and net worth you attest to on the funding portal; the portal, not Harvest, is responsible for tracking your cumulative Reg CF investments across all issuers in a rolling 12-month window, since the $2,500-to-$124,000 cap described in [Regulatory Pathways](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#route-b--reg-cf-retail-participation) applies across every Reg CF deal you're in, not just this one.

## Step 3 — What you're actually buying

You are buying a **membership interest in one named Series** of Harvest Fleet I, LLC — not stock in Harvest Operating Co., not a claim on the whole company, and not a claim on any Series other than the one you invested in. Per [the structure](../machine-shares#structure), that Series is a defined pool of collection cells at a named site, and your interest entitles you to a pro-rata share of that Series' distributable cash, calculated by [the waterfall](../machine-shares#what-holders-get) — nothing else. You have no vote on operations, task programs, or pricing, and the subscription documents will say so explicitly, because that separation is what keeps the structure's economics clean (see [Regulatory Pathways](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#start-from-the-honest-answer) on why holder passivity is a deliberate design choice, not an oversight).

## Step 4 — Funding

ACH or wire, run through the transfer agent's escrow. Funds are held in escrow until the Series' raise target is met (or the offering's minimum, if a rolling close applies) — this is standard practice across every route and protects you from funding a Series that never actually gets built. If a Series doesn't reach its funding minimum by the stated deadline, funds are returned in full; no cells get financed by a partially-funded Series.

## Step 5 — What you receive, and when

* **At closing:** a fully executed copy of your subscription agreement and the Series' operating agreement, held with the transfer agent and accessible on demand — this is your proof of ownership, whether or not a token layer exists yet.
* **Monthly:** per-cell operating data for your Series — uptime, collected hours, accepted episodes, acceptance rate, sell-through — the same reporting cadence described in [Machine Shares](../machine-shares#what-holders-get). You are watching the machine work, not waiting for a quarterly letter to find out.
* **Quarterly:** a distribution, if the Series generated distributable cash, with the waterfall arithmetic shown — not just a number, but the calculation that produced it — plus a maintenance-reserve position statement.
* **Annually:** an independent review of revenue attribution against delivery manifests, and your tax documents (see below).

## Step 6 — Tax treatment

Machine Shares are membership interests in an LLC, not shares of stock — the tax treatment follows the same K-1 path as AcreTrader's per-property structure (see [Comparable Models](../comparable-models#farmland-tokenization-honest-yield-different-asset-physics)), not a 1099. You receive a **Schedule K-1** annually reflecting your pro-rata share of the Series' income, deductions, and — this matters for a depreciating asset — your share of the **depreciation pass-through** on the collection cells themselves. Depreciation is a real tax benefit specific to this structure: it can offset distributed income in the early years of a Series' life, which is one of the reasons a fixed-payment note (Route D) and a Machine Share are taxed differently even when the cash yield looks similar. This is general information, not tax advice — a K-1 investment changes how you file, and holders should expect to involve a tax preparer familiar with pass-through entities.

## Step 7 — Liquidity, stated plainly

This is the question every comp in [Comparable Models](comparable-models) gets asked, and the honest answer is the same one [Machine Shares](../machine-shares#why-it-might-not-work) already gives: **there is no public secondary market at launch.** Your capital is committed for the life of the Series — nominally its 24-month depreciation schedule, extending toward the 36-month design life as residual value is realized — unless one of the following applies:

* **A private secondary sale**, subject to the Series' transfer restrictions and, where required, right-of-first-refusal provisions — comparable to AcreTrader's post-year-one private-sale path, not a listed exchange.
* **A future compliant token layer**, described in [Token Architecture](token-architecture), which is the only path to anything resembling an active secondary market — and even then, only after transfer restrictions are enforceable and eligibility can be checked programmatically, per the guardrails in [Regulatory Pathways](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-token-layer).

**If you need this capital back on a schedule you control, this is not the right instrument.** Every comp in this category that has gotten into trouble — Lofty's condemned-property lawsuit is the sharpest example in [Comparable Models](../comparable-models#real-estate-tokenization-the-marketing-to-distribution-gap) — got there partly by overselling liquidity a token listing didn't actually deliver. Machine Shares makes no such promise, on purpose.

## Step 8 — What happens at Series wind-up

At the end of a Series' operating life, cells are either redeployed into a successor Series (with holders offered a rollover option) or sold on the secondary hardware market referenced in [Machine Shares](../machine-shares#the-unit) — the Unitree G1 EDU has an active resale market, which is part of what makes the residual-value line in [the comparison table](../machine-shares#why-the-yield-story-is-clean) real rather than aspirational. Net sale proceeds, after the maintenance reserve is settled, are distributed through the same waterfall as ordinary distributions. A full walk-through of the numbers behind this — including a worked example at two ticket sizes — is in [Offering Economics](../internal-not-for-publication/offering-economics).

## Frequently asked, answered directly

**Can I choose which cells or site I'm invested in?** Yes, at the Series level — each Series maps to one named site, and the offering materials will identify it. You cannot select individual cells within a Series; that granularity is exactly what [the structure](../machine-shares#structure) argues against.

**What if the Series doesn't sell through its capacity?** You receive nothing that quarter, and the maintenance reserve continues to accrue against the Series' assets. This is the Year 1 and Bear row in [the yield model](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-yield-model), and it is why Harvest's stated policy is to never offer a Series before its cells have contracted or reserved demand behind them.

**Is my investment insured or guaranteed?** No. It is an equity-like interest in a depreciating industrial asset with real operating risk. The cells themselves carry asset-level insurance per [Machine Shares](../machine-shares#what-holders-get), which protects the Series' balance sheet against physical loss — it does not guarantee your return.

**Who do I contact with questions once I'm a holder?** The transfer agent handles account and document access; Series-specific operating questions route through Harvest's investor relations function, established before any Series opens to holders.

# Why This Yield Story Is Cleaner Than the Comps

[Machine Shares](machine-shares) makes the claim directly: this is a cleaner yield story than almost anything else marketed as a real-world asset. That claim is worth nothing without naming the comps and showing the arithmetic. This page does that — four categories, real numbers, current as of September 2026.

## Real estate tokenization: the marketing-to-distribution gap

**Lofty** is the clearest cautionary tale in the category, and it is instructive precisely because its structure looks a lot like ours on paper: single-asset LLCs, fractional tokens, revenue distributed to holders.

The gap is between what is marketed and what is paid. Lofty's marketplace advertises an average yield around 9–11%, with some property-level IRRs marketed north of 24%. Independent reviews of actual investor experience report that **distributions have not matched those projections** on typical holdings. Layer on the transaction economics: a 2.5% buy fee, a 3% sell fee, additional market-order surcharges, and a realistic round trip — buy when convenient, sell when you need the cash — costs roughly **8% of the position**, on top of any yield shortfall.

The regulatory foundation is the second problem. Lofty's retail marketplace runs on a Wyoming LLC plus Algorand tokenization theory that has not been tested by enforcement or by a hard market event. There is no SEC registration at the individual property level. When something does go wrong — a condemned property in Akron, Ohio, and the lawsuit that followed — the untested structure is exactly where the exposure concentrates.

**What this means for Machine Shares:** the [Regulatory Pathways](../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield) page starts from "this is almost certainly a security" and builds through well-trodden Reg D / Reg CF / Reg A+ exemptions specifically to avoid Lofty's foundational bet. And every yield figure in [the yield model](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-yield-model) is presented with its failure case in the same table — Year 1 and Bear both show **0%** — rather than leading with the optimistic case and hoping the gap goes unnoticed.

## Farmland tokenization: honest yield, different asset physics

**AcreTrader** is the closer structural cousin, and it is the comp Machine Shares should be benchmarked against rather than caricatured next to.

AcreTrader pays a real, modest cash yield — **3–5% annually**, distributed once a year in December — on top of land appreciation that has historically averaged around 11.5% a year from 1990–2018 (explicitly not a forward guarantee). Structure: a separate LLC per property, investors hold partnership interests taxed on a Schedule K-1, 100% debt-free ownership of the underlying asset, a 2% closing fee and a 0.75% annual management fee. Minimum tickets run $15,000–$40,000. Standard hold is 3–5 years, with early exit only through a private secondary sale after year one.

This is the same Series-per-asset, K-1, no-token-required playbook that [the Series LLC section](../machine-shares#structure) is built on. The honest difference is the underlying asset's physics: **farmland doesn't depreciate — collection cells do.** AcreTrader's low single-digit cash yield is acceptable to its holders because the land itself is the store of value and the yield is a bonus. A Collection Unit is a 24–36 month depreciating industrial asset; its yield has to do the work that AcreTrader's land appreciation does, which is exactly why [the yield model](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-yield-model) insists a holder read Year 2's 21.1% as **return of capital plus return on capital**, not a perpetual coupon, and why the maintenance reserve and residual-value mechanics matter as much as the headline number.

## Solar income funds: the accredited-only precedent that actually paid out

**Wunder Capital** is worth naming because it is the cleanest historical precedent for "asset-secured, accredited-only, fixed-cadence distributions" — the exact shape of [Route A, Reg D 506(c)](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#route-a--reg-d-506c-accredited-only).

Wunder ran several funds against pools of commercial-scale solar installations, each loan secured by the physical solar assets it financed: a Term Fund targeting **8.5% annual** cashflow over 7 years, a 5 Fund targeting **7.5% annual** over 5 years, an Income Fund targeting **6% annual** over 10 years, distributed monthly, accredited investors only. No token, no public marketplace, no secondary-liquidity promise — just a lien on a physical, revenue-producing asset and a fixed payment schedule.

That is close to what Route D (debt, or a fixed-payment lease) would look like for a Collection Unit — a legitimate, lower-story alternative to the profit-participation structure Machine Shares actually is. The reason Machine Shares chooses profit participation over a Wunder-style fixed note is the same reason it accepts the securities-law burden: **a 21% base-case gross yield on 35% profit share is a materially better outcome than a fixed 6–8.5% note**, and the asset (a 24-month machine, not a 20-year solar array) can support that upside because the revenue itself, not the loan, is what's being sold.

## DePIN robotics tokenomics: the comp that should worry every reader

This is the category most likely to get Machine Shares lumped in by a skeptical reader, and it is also the category with the worst-documented gap between token rewards and real revenue.

The data, drawn from an independent analysis of Solana DePIN networks through Q1 2026: **Hivemapper's** monthly revenue fell from $195K in December to roughly $6K in March — a 97% collapse — while its contributor count _grew_ 36.2% over the same period. Contributors kept showing up and getting paid while the underlying demand for the data they were producing evaporated. That combination — falling revenue, rising payouts — has one explanation: **the rewards are coming from token emissions, not from buyers.** **Render** shows the same pattern in miniature: an 80% revenue collapse from a December peak, with contributor counts holding roughly steady, implying reward pools were diluted rather than cut. Of the three networks studied, only **Helium Mobile** showed a defensible link between revenue and reward — a stable \~$188K in March with a modest $15.60 average reward per contributor, tied to a recurring, demand-driven use case (mobile connectivity offload) rather than speculative collection.

This is precisely the failure mode [Machine Shares](../machine-shares#why-the-yield-story-is-clean) names and refuses to build: _"Depends on token price: No."_ A Machine Share's distribution is a fixed percentage of dollars a named collection unit was paid by an enterprise buyer under contract — visible in [the delivery manifest](https://github.com/karnrajsinghchauhan/harvest-docs/tree/main/the-data-business/delivery-format.md), auditable against [the yield model](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-yield-model)'s own worst case, which is **zero, not negative-but-hidden-by-emissions.** If Harvest's Series ever underperforms, holders see a $0 distribution and a maintenance-reserve call — not a token price quietly absorbing the shortfall while a dashboard keeps showing green.

The two DePIN robotics-specific precedents cited in [Regulatory Pathways](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-token-layer) — XMAQUINA's machine-RWA DAO on peaq and PrismaX's staked teleoperation network — are the more honest cousins in this category: XMAQUINA pairs its DEUS token with a real reported treasury and a planned regulatory sandbox rather than an unbacked emissions schedule, and PrismaX ties rewards to an automated Eval Engine scoring actual work quality. Both are still earlier and less proven than Route A. Neither is a reason to skip the non-token version first.

## Institutional tokenization infrastructure: the rails are being built right now

The one piece of the landscape that has changed materially since [Regulatory Pathways](../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield) was first drafted: **on August 31, 2026, Intercontinental Exchange — the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange — took a stake in tZERO and licensed its 103-patent blockchain portfolio**, with tZERO set to become the digital transfer agent on an NYSE-affiliated tokenized-securities platform, handling settlement and ownership tracking for tokenized trades under SEC-compliant rails. Citi's own research, cited in the same coverage, projects the tokenized-securities market could reach **$5.5 trillion by 2030**.

This does not change the recommendation in [Regulatory Pathways](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#recommendation) — Route A under Reg D, today, with a Delaware Series LLC — but it does change the credibility of "add a token layer later." A year ago, a transfer-agent-grade tokenization rail meant choosing between a handful of crypto-native platforms with regulatory theories of varying strength. Now the operator of the NYSE itself is building one. **If and when Machine Shares adds** [**a token layer**](token-architecture)**, it will be adding it onto infrastructure that Wall Street, not just crypto-native platforms, is now underwriting.**

## The comparison, side by side

| Platform                   | Asset                | Stated yield                                                 | What actually happens                                                               | Structure                                                         |
| -------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Lofty (real estate)        | Rental property      | 9–11% marketed, up to 24% IRR claimed                        | Distributions run below projections; \~8% round-trip friction                       | Wyoming LLC + untested token theory                               |
| AcreTrader (farmland)      | Land                 | 3–5% cash + historical \~11.5%/yr appreciation               | Paid annually, land doesn't depreciate                                              | Per-property LLC, K-1, debt-free                                  |
| Wunder Capital (solar)     | Solar installations  | 6–8.5% fixed                                                 | Paid monthly, asset-secured note                                                    | Accredited-only, fixed note                                       |
| Hivemapper (DePIN)         | Mapping data         | Variable token rewards                                       | Revenue fell 97%, payouts kept rising — emissions, not demand                       | Public token, no securities wrapper                               |
| **Harvest Machine Shares** | **Collection cells** | **0% / 21.1% / 47.8% by scenario, all three shown together** | **A dollar figure tied to a delivery manifest, or zero — never emissions-smoothed** | **Series LLC, Reg D → CF → A+, token optional and additive only** |

The pattern across every comp above is the same: **the platforms that survive scrutiny show their bad case next to their good case, and the ones that don't, don't.** [The yield model](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-yield-model) is built the first way on purpose.

# Token Architecture

[Regulatory Pathways](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-token-layer) sets the rule: a token layer, if added, represents a transfer-restricted Series interest and never becomes the source of yield. This page is the technical design that follows from that rule — what a compliant token layer actually consists of, which vendor category does which job, and why the sequencing matters.

## The rule restated as a system constraint

Every component below exists to do exactly one of two things: **represent** an already-legally-real interest, or **enforce** a rule that already exists in the operating agreement. Nothing below creates a new economic right. If a design decision would make the token itself a source of value independent of the underlying Series interest, it is out of scope by definition — that is the line [Comparable Models](../comparable-models#depin-robotics-tokenomics-the-comp-that-should-worry-every-reader) shows getting crossed, repeatedly, in the DePIN category.

## The four layers

```
   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  LEGAL LAYER                                        │
   │  Series LLC operating agreement · subscription docs │
   │  This is the actual interest. Everything below       │
   │  points back to this, nothing replaces it.           │
   └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
   ┌───────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐
   │  TRANSFER AGENT LAYER                                │
   │  legally authoritative record of who owns what        │
   │  enforces eligibility + transfer restrictions          │
   └───────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
   ┌──────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐
   │  TOKEN / SETTLEMENT LAYER                             │
   │  on-chain representation, mirrors the transfer agent   │
   │  enables compliant secondary transfer + distribution   │
   └───────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
   ┌───────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐
   │  HOLDER-FACING LAYER                                  │
   │  wallet or custodial account · reporting dashboard     │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Legal layer

Unchanged by anything below it. The Series LLC operating agreement is the actual instrument; the subscription agreement is what a holder signs; [Offering Economics](../../internal-not-for-publication/offering-economics#the-waterfall-expanded) is the arithmetic it entitles a holder to. A token that stopped existing tomorrow would not change what a holder owns — that property is the test for whether the token layer is designed correctly.

### Transfer agent layer

This is the layer that changed materially in 2026. Historically, a company building this had to choose between crypto-native platforms — **Securitize** and **tZERO** are the two most established — each running its own regulatory theory for how an on-chain record interoperates with a legally authoritative cap table. As of **August 31, 2026, that category gained a very different kind of validation**: Intercontinental Exchange, the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, took a stake in tZERO and licensed its 103-patent blockchain portfolio, with tZERO becoming the digital transfer agent on an NYSE-affiliated tokenized-securities platform — handling settlement and ownership tracking under SEC-compliant rails, pending regulatory approval. Citi's research, cited in the same announcement, projects the tokenized-securities market reaching **$5.5 trillion by 2030**. See [Comparable Models](../comparable-models#institutional-tokenization-infrastructure-the-rails-are-being-built-right-now) for the full context.

What a transfer agent actually does here, regardless of which one is chosen: maintains the **legally authoritative** record of who owns what interest in which Series, enforces **eligibility rules** programmatically (accredited-only for a 506(c) Series, per-investor caps for a Reg CF Series), enforces the **holding period and transfer restrictions** the exemption requires, and processes any secondary transfer through a compliant workflow rather than a peer-to-peer handoff. If the token layer and the transfer agent's record ever disagree, **the transfer agent's record controls** — the token is a representation, and representations can lag or be re-synced; the underlying interest cannot.

### Token / settlement layer

The optional on-chain component, and the one that should be added last, not first. Its legitimate functions, restated from [Regulatory Pathways](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-token-layer):

* **Transfer-restricted representation** of a Series interest — a wallet address can hold it, but the smart contract itself checks eligibility against the transfer agent's record before allowing any movement.
* **Programmable compliance** — holding-period locks, accreditation-gate checks, and per-investor cap enforcement encoded at the contract level rather than relying on a human reviewing every transfer request.
* **Stablecoin settlement of distributions** — a quarterly distribution calculation (per [Offering Economics](../../internal-not-for-publication/offering-economics#the-waterfall-expanded)) can trigger a stablecoin payout to verified holder wallets automatically, which is a genuine operational improvement over ACH batch runs for a large, geographically distributed holder base.
* **A compliant secondary venue**, once transfer restrictions are technically enforceable — this is the closest thing to the liquidity [the Investor Guide](../investor-guide#step-7--liquidity-stated-plainly) says does not exist at launch, and it is explicitly a Phase 2 capability, not a launch feature.

What it must never do, restated as hard constraints on the contract design: no function that lets token price diverge from the Series interest it represents; no mechanism — staking rewards, emissions, liquidity-mining — that pays holders anything not sourced from [Series Distributable Cash](../../internal-not-for-publication/offering-economics#the-waterfall-expanded); no public minting or listing before transfer restrictions are live and tested; no marketing that implies the token is more liquid or more valuable than the legal interest underneath it.

### Holder-facing layer

Most holders should not need to think about which layer they're interacting with. A custodial account — holding the token on the investor's behalf, the way a brokerage holds shares in "street name" — is the right default for a Reg CF or Reg D holder who wants the reporting dashboard from [the Investor Guide](../investor-guide#step-5--what-you-receive-and-when) without managing a self-custody wallet and a seed phrase. A self-custody option can exist for holders who specifically want it, gated behind the same eligibility checks as everything else.

## Sequencing: why this is Phase 2, not launch

[Regulatory Pathways](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#recommendation) is unambiguous: **Route A, Reg D 506(c), today, with a Delaware Series LLC and a securities lawyer** — no token required to do any of that. The token architecture above is real and buildable, but building it before Series A has a distribution track record inverts the priority [the Investor Guide](../investor-guide#step-1--which-route-applies-to-you) and [Offering Economics](../../internal-not-for-publication/offering-economics#the-series-lifecycle) both assume: prove the waterfall pays out correctly on a small, accredited, low-drama Series first. A token layer added to an unproven Series doesn't fix the proof problem — it just adds smart-contract risk and a second regulatory surface to an offering that hasn't yet demonstrated its core promise.

The realistic timeline, consistent with [the precedent](../../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield#the-precedent-to-learn-from-rather-than-copy) of XMAQUINA's and PrismaX's jurisdictional-engagement-first approach: **6–12 months** from "Series A is distributing correctly" to "a compliant token layer is live," not a sprint bolted onto the initial raise. The institutional rails being built by ICE and tZERO make that 6–12 month window a better bet in September 2026 than it would have been a year earlier — but they don't shorten it, and they don't remove the requirement to get Route A right first.

# Stake-to-Collect

> **Status: design document.** Not an offer, not a commitment. Any implementation involving a token requires securities and money-transmission counsel before launch.

## The problem this solves

The [Unit Economics](../internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics) show that operator labour is 55% of onshore cost and that acceptance rate is the second-largest lever on margin. Both point at the same underlying issue: **we pay for collected hours and we sell usable hours, and the operator controls the ratio between them.**

An hourly wage pays identically for a 90%-acceptance operator and a 55%-acceptance operator. That is a straightforwardly bad incentive. Piece rates fix it and introduce a worse one — paying per accepted episode rewards volume over difficulty, and operators will route themselves to the easiest task classes and rush the hard ones, which destroys exactly the distributional diversity the corpus is sold for.

**Stake-to-collect is a third option: a refundable quality bond.**

## The mechanism

```
  1  QUALIFY    operator passes the calibration set against a golden reference
  2  STAKE      operator posts a refundable bond, sized to their access tier
  3  COLLECT    operator claims task programs; higher tiers unlock higher rates
  4  GRADE      QA gates run; acceptance recorded per episode
  5  SETTLE     base rate + quality bonus paid; stake adjusted on the outcome
  6  TIER       sustained performance raises tier, stake requirement and rate
```

### The stake

| Tier            | Stake  | Access                                                                | Base rate       | Quality bonus at ≥85% acceptance |
| --------------- | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------- | -------------------------------- |
| **Provisional** | $0     | Training tasks only, 100% reviewed                                    | Standard hourly | —                                |
| **Qualified**   | $250   | Standard programs                                                     | Standard hourly | +10%                             |
| **Senior**      | $750   | Contact-rich and precision programs                                   | +15%            | +20%                             |
| **Principal**   | $2,000 | Buyer-facing programs, failure-injection work, calibration authorship | +30%            | +25%                             |

The stake is **posted by Harvest on the operator's behalf** at qualification, and vests to the operator over their first 500 accepted episodes. This is the design choice that makes the whole thing defensible:

> **Operators never pay to work.** The stake is a retention and quality instrument funded by Harvest, not a barrier funded by the worker.

An operator who leaves before vesting forfeits the unvested portion back to Harvest. An operator whose acceptance falls below the tier floor for two consecutive cycles has a portion of the stake slashed against the cost of the rejected work, capped at 25% per cycle, and drops a tier. An operator who leaves after vesting takes the stake with them.

**Any structure where a worker must post their own capital to access work is a structure we do not build.** It transfers business risk onto the lowest-paid participant, and it is the fastest route to becoming the cautionary tale described in the [Risk Register](../../internal-not-for-publication/risk-register#labour-and-reputational-exposure).

### The grading

Slashing on a subjective judgement is corrosive. Grading is therefore mechanical and appealable:

* **Gates 1 and 2 are fully automated** — integrity and kinematic sanity, deterministic, no human discretion, and the operator sees the failure reason within minutes.
* **Gate 3 is model-assisted with human review**, and only Gate 3 rejections above a threshold rate trigger slashing.
* **Every operator can appeal an episode-level rejection.** Appeals are reviewed by someone who is not the original reviewer. Sustained appeals restore the stake and correct the operator's record.
* **Corpus-level rejections never slash.** If a program fails a diversity audit that is a task-design failure and it is ours.

Publishing that last rule matters more than it looks. It tells operators exactly where the boundary of their responsibility sits, and it is the difference between a quality system and an arbitrary one.

## Why this beats both alternatives

|                                             | Hourly  | Piece rate                  | Stake-to-collect                  |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Rewards quality                             | No      | Partially                   | **Yes, directly**                 |
| Rewards hard tasks                          | Neutral | **No — actively penalizes** | Yes, via tier access              |
| Operator income stability                   | High    | Low                         | **High** — base rate is preserved |
| Retention incentive                         | Weak    | Weak                        | **Strong** — vesting schedule     |
| Protects the 20–40 hour training investment | No      | No                          | **Yes**                           |
| Worker bears business risk                  | No      | Partially                   | **No** — Harvest funds the stake  |

The retention property is the underrated one. A trained operator represents 20–40 hours of investment before they are consistently good. A vesting stake makes that investment mutual, and turns operator tenure from an HR metric into an asset on the balance sheet.

## Two designs we are not building, and why

**Open permissionless collection.** Anyone stakes, connects any robot, collects anything. The precedents exist — PrismaX operates a teleoperation coordination layer where operators stake network tokens for trust and access to higher-paying tasks, with rewards tied to work quality as well as stake size, backed by an automated Eval Engine scoring trajectories without human validators. BitRobot, from FrodoBots Labs with Protocol Labs, crowdsources robot data through public teleoperation with verifiable-work tokens.

These are genuinely interesting and they solve a different problem. They optimize for **scale and diversity of contributors**. Harvest's product is **controlled provenance and calibrated environments** — a warrantable chain of custody in US facilities, which is one of the three things we said price deflation cannot reach. Opening collection to unverified contributors and uncontrolled environments destroys the thing we sell. **We could build a second product line that does this. We should not make it the same product line.**

**A public token from day one.** Regulatory exposure, a launch problem, a market-making problem and a governance problem — in exchange for capital we can raise more cheaply and a distribution effect we do not yet need. See the position below.

## Regulatory position

Two questions matter and they have different answers.

### Is the stake a security?

**As designed here: no, and by construction.** The operator does not invest their own money — Harvest funds the stake. There is no expectation of profit from others' efforts; there is compensation for the operator's own labour. It is a **refundable performance bond in an employment or contractor relationship**, a structure with a very long history in staffing and construction.

The elements that would flip it, any one of which is disqualifying:

* Operators purchasing the stake themselves → investment of money
* The stake appreciating independently of work performed → expectation of profit
* Returns to stakers who do not themselves collect → profit from the efforts of others
* A tradeable secondary market in stakes → the tell that it has become an investment product

**The last one is the bright line.** A refundable bond that cannot be traded is a bond. Make it tradeable and it becomes something to be analyzed under Howey, and the analysis will not go well.

### Is this employment?

Almost certainly. Tiering, scheduling, quality standards, training requirements and equipment provision are the classic indicia of employment under both federal and state tests — and California's ABC test is stricter still.

**The recommended position: treat operators as employees and stop looking for a way around it.** It is more expensive, it is already priced into the $32/hour fully-loaded onshore figure in [Unit Economics](../internal-not-for-publication/unit-economics), and it is a direct input to the provenance warranty we sell at a premium. A vendor whose collection chain is under labour-classification challenge cannot warrant provenance to an enterprise buyer.

The industry's cautionary tale is close at hand: a competitor deploying headsets through India's gig economy is being examined by India's Ministry of Electronics and IT over consent mechanisms, and two major Indian gig platforms declined to partner over privacy concerns. **We should be able to point at that and say: this is the reason our model is what it is.**

## If a token is ever added

Only after the non-token version has run for a year and works. The narrow, defensible use:

* **A record, not an instrument.** On-chain attestation of operator qualification, tier and accepted-episode count — a portable, verifiable work history the operator owns and can take with them.
* **Settlement rail**, if stablecoin settlement is genuinely better for a distributed operator pool than existing payroll infrastructure. Frequently it is not.
* **Never** a tradeable claim on Harvest revenue. That is a [Machine Share](machine-shares), it is a security, and it belongs in that structure with that structure's exemption.

A portable, verifiable operator credential is a genuinely good idea that happens to suit a ledger. It is also worth building without one. **If the credential is only interesting because it is tokenized, it was not interesting.**

## What to build first

Nothing on this page requires a token, a blockchain, or a lawyer beyond ordinary employment counsel:

1. **The calibration set and golden reference** — required regardless, and the single highest-value QA investment in the business
2. **Tiering with rate differentials** — a payroll configuration
3. **The vesting quality bond, Harvest-funded** — a compensation design
4. **Automated Gate 1 and 2 feedback within minutes** — an engineering task, and the thing operators will value most
5. **The appeals process** — a policy document

That is the whole mechanism. Everything valuable here is available without any of the machinery the name suggests.

# Legal & Corporate Overview

Harvest sells two things that both create legal exposure before they create revenue: physical robots operating in shared or leased space, and data products built from footage and motion capture of the people operating them. This section is the paper that has to exist before either of those can scale past a handful of pilot cells.

**Read this first:** every document in this section is a working draft written to be legally coherent and internally consistent, not a filed or attorney-reviewed instrument. Nothing here is legal advice, and nothing here should be signed, relied on in a dispute, or represented to a counterparty as final until a licensed attorney in the relevant jurisdiction has reviewed it. Treat this section as the first draft that saves counsel the most expensive hours — scoping and structure — not as a replacement for counsel.

### What's in here

* [Terms of Service](terms-of-service) — governs use of the Harvest website, docs site, and any buyer-facing delivery portal.
* [Privacy Policy](privacy-policy) — what Harvest collects from site visitors, buyers, and operators, and how teleoperation footage of human operators is handled.
* [Data License Agreement](data-license-agreement) — the commercial contract a buyer signs to receive a dataset. This is the paper behind the pricing model in [Pricing, Licensing and Contracts](../the-data-business/pricing-licensing).
* [Operator Agreement](operator-agreement) — the contract every human teleoperator signs before entering a collection cell: IP assignment, consent, likeness rights, safety, and pay.
* [IP & Data Ownership Policy](ip-data-ownership) — who owns what, at every stage from raw footage to a licensed episode, including third-party IP embedded in the pipeline (robot firmware, foundation models, annotation tools).
* [Export Control & Compliance](export-control) — the ITAR/EAR and CFIUS-adjacent questions that follow directly from operating and re-exporting data about a foreign-manufactured humanoid robot. Reads alongside [Compliance and Procurement Risk](../platform/compliance-risk).
* [Insurance & Liability Framework](insurance-liability) — coverage lines a robotics data operator actually needs, and the liability allocation between Harvest, operators, buyers, and site hosts.

### Entity structure (as designed)

Harvest operates as a US-registered entity (the "Company") with a single class of data-collection and licensing operations. Two structures referenced elsewhere in this book sit outside the core entity's ordinary-course contracts and carry their own legal treatment:

* **Machine Shares** ([Machine Shares: Fractional Robot Ownership](../capital-structures/machine-shares)) — fractional economic interests in named collection units, structured through one of the four routes analyzed in [Regulatory Pathways and the Yield Model](../internal-not-for-publication/regulatory-yield). These are securities offerings and are not covered by the commercial contracts in this Legal section.
* **Stake-to-Collect** ([Stake-to-Collect](../capital-structures/stake-to-collect)) — an operator staking mechanism with its own regulatory line, addressed in that page directly.

Everything else — the corporate shell, the buyer contracts, the operator contracts, the insurance program — is ordinary-course and is what this section covers.

### Open items

* Registered agent, cap table, and formation documents are not modeled here — they are jurisdiction- and founder-specific and belong in a corporate minute book, not a public-facing docs site.
* No document in this section has been reviewed by outside counsel as of this writing.
* Export control treatment ([Export Control & Compliance](export-control)) is the single highest-priority legal item on the [Risk Register](../internal-not-for-publication/risk-register) — it should be the first thing a retained attorney looks at.

# Privacy Policy

_Draft template. Not legal advice. Have counsel review against CCPA/CPRA, applicable state privacy laws, and — if any buyer or operator activity touches the EU/UK — GDPR before publishing._

**Last updated:** \[date] · **Controller:** Harvest \[Corp / Inc.]

Harvest's data footprint has two very different categories that this policy has to keep separate: ordinary web/business data (site visitors, buyer contacts, prospects) and the teleoperation footage of human operators that forms the basis of the training-data product. The second category is the one every buyer's legal team will ask about, and this policy treats it as such.

### 1. Information we collect

**From site visitors and prospects:** contact details submitted through forms or outreach (name, email, company), usage analytics on the documentation and marketing site (page views, referrers, approximate location from IP), and any information shared during sales conversations.

**From buyers:** billing and contracting details, authorized-user contacts for the delivery portal, and usage logs of dataset access (what was downloaded, when, by whom) for license-compliance purposes.

**From operators (teleoperators):** the [Operator Agreement](operator-agreement) governs this in full; this policy summarizes it. Operators generate video, audio (where enabled), and motion/force/proprioception data of themselves while teleoperating a G1 unit inside a collection cell. This is personal data under most privacy frameworks because it can identify the operator (visually, or via gait/motion signature). We collect it only inside consented collection sessions, never covertly, and never outside the physical bounds of a Harvest cell.

### 2. How we use it

Site and buyer data: to operate the Services, respond to inquiries, deliver licensed datasets, invoice, and maintain security logs. Operator data: to produce, QA, annotate, and license training-data episodes under the format described in [Delivery Format and the QA Gate](../the-data-business/delivery-format), and — only with the specific consent captured in the Operator Agreement — to appear in Harvest's own marketing material (e.g., demo video footage).

We do not sell personal data in the sense used by CCPA/CPRA. Licensing a dataset containing operator footage to a buyer is a data license, not a personal-data sale, but the two can look similar to a regulator and this distinction needs counsel's sign-off on the actual notice language before publication.

### 3. Legal basis and consent

Operator data is processed on the basis of the operator's signed consent in the Operator Agreement, which is granular: separate consent lines exist for (a) inclusion in licensed training datasets, (b) inclusion in Harvest's own marketing/demo content, and (c) any future use not contemplated at signing, which requires re-consent. Buyer and site-visitor data is processed on the basis of contract performance and legitimate interest.

### 4. Sharing and disclosure

We share operator-derived data with licensed buyers strictly within the scope of an executed Data License Agreement, with subprocessors that support hosting, annotation tooling, and delivery infrastructure under written data-processing terms, and with legal or regulatory authorities where required by law. We do not share personal data with data brokers or for cross-context behavioral advertising.

### 5. Retention

Raw, unannotated footage is retained only as long as needed to produce the licensed episode and pass QA, per the retention window defined operationally in [The G1 Capture Stack](../the-data-business/capture-stack). Licensed episode data is retained per the term of the applicable Data License Agreement. Operator consent records are retained for the life of the operator relationship plus the statutory period required to defend a claim.

### 6. Operator and buyer rights

Operators may request access to correction of, or deletion of their personal data, subject to Harvest's ability to fulfill deletion without breaching an already-executed Data License Agreement covering episodes their footage appears in — this tension is disclosed to operators at signing, not discovered later. California residents and residents of other applicable states have statutory rights (access, deletion, correction, opt-out of sale/sharing) exercisable via \[privacy@harvest.co — to be finalized].

### 7. Security

See [Data Security & Access Control](../security/security) for the technical and organizational measures protecting this data end to end, from cell capture through buyer delivery.

### 8. International transfers

If any collection, annotation, or buyer activity crosses borders, a transfer mechanism (SCCs or equivalent) must be documented before that flow goes live. As of this writing, collection operations are US-only per company policy.

### 9. Children's data

The Services and collection operations are not directed at, and do not knowingly collect data from, individuals under 18.

### 10. Changes and contact

Material changes will be reflected here with an updated date. Questions or requests: \[privacy@harvest.co — to be finalized].

# IP & Data Ownership Policy

_Draft template. Not legal advice._ This page maps who owns what at every stage of the pipeline described in [Robot to Buyer: the full pipeline](../the-data-business/data-business) — it is the internal reference the other legal documents point back to.

### The chain of title, stage by stage

**1. Raw footage (captured in the cell).** Owned by Harvest from the moment of capture, by assignment under Section 3 of the [Operator Agreement](operator-agreement). The Operator retains personality/likeness rights, separately licensed under Section 4 of that agreement — ownership of the recording and rights over the person depicted in it are legally distinct, and this policy treats them as such throughout.

**2. Annotated episode (post-QA, in GR00T LeRobot format).** Owned by Harvest. Annotation layers (task labels, success/failure flags, modality metadata per [Delivery Format and the QA Gate](../the-data-business/delivery-format)) are Harvest's original work product, whether produced by human annotators or by the [annotation agents](../ai-agents-and-autonomy/ai-agents) described in the AI Agents section — output from an automated agent Harvest operates and directs is Harvest's work product, not the tool vendor's.

**3. Licensed dataset (delivered to a buyer).** The buyer receives a license, not ownership, of the episode data — see Section 2 of the [Data License Agreement](data-license-agreement). Harvest retains underlying ownership and may license the same episodes to other buyers unless an exclusivity term applies.

**4. Derivative Model (a buyer's trained policy).** Owned entirely by the buyer. Harvest asserts no claim over models trained on licensed data — this is a deliberate boundary stated explicitly in the Data License Agreement (Section 2) and repeated here because it is the single most common point of buyer legal diligence: _does Harvest claim any downstream IP in what we build with this?_ No.

### Third-party IP embedded in the stack

* **Unitree G1 firmware and hardware design** — owned by Unitree; Harvest's rights are limited to use under the terms of purchase/lease, addressed in [Compliance and Procurement Risk](../platform/compliance-risk). No Unitree IP is sublicensed to buyers; buyers receive Harvest's data output, not the robot's design.
* **GR00T LeRobot format** — an open specification; Harvest's conformance to it is a delivery-format choice, not a license Harvest needs to pass through.
* **Annotation and orchestration tooling** — where Harvest uses third-party or open-source models to run the agents described in [AI Agents & Autonomy](../ai-agents-and-autonomy/ai-agents), the license terms of each tool (commercial API terms, or open-source license) govern Harvest's right to use that tool internally; none of those licenses attach to the output data itself unless the tool's terms specifically say so, which must be checked per vendor.

### Company IP

Harvest's own inventions — the capture cell design, the QA pipeline, the agent orchestration logic, the Machine Shares and Stake-to-Collect structures — are Company IP. Contractors and vendors (e.g., the video-production vendor referenced in the collection-marketing workflow) assign work product to Harvest under their own engagement terms, which should mirror Section 3 of the Operator Agreement for any contractor whose output could plausibly be claimed as their own.

### Open items

* No patent strategy is modeled here — if the capture-cell design or an agent-orchestration method is genuinely novel, a provisional filing decision should be made before it's publicly described in more detail than this page already does.
* Trademark clearance and registration for "Harvest" as used in commerce has not been confirmed.
